sections.title: About This Guide
sections.content:
# About This Guide

## What is this about?

Standard advice on learning often fails the people who need it most. We are frequently told that to practice we must spend many hours repeating the same thing many times and that this will eventually lead to mastery, but rarely are we told **how** to spend those hours. Many dedicated learners simply repeat the same mistakes for years rather than correcting them. They hit plateaus and eventually give up, assuming they simply lack the necessary talent. This guide addresses that specific gap.

Most existing literature on "Deliberate Practice" focuses on elite performers—chess grandmasters, Olympic athletes, or concert violinists—who have access to world-class coaches and established training programs. That advice is useless if you are trying to improve your academic writing alone in a library or learning a foreign language without a tutor. I wanted to translate the principles of high-performance psychology into a practical toolkit for anybody.

> This guide is an attempt to democratize expertise. It takes the methods used by expert performers working with world-class coaches and adapts them for individuals working on their own and directing their own learning in contexts where resources are scarce.

## Who this is for

This book is for anyone currently stuck on a plateau. You might be an academic writer struggling to turn complex thoughts into clear text, a language learner who understands grammar rules but freezes in conversation, or a musician who can play the notes but lacks fluency. You do not need to be aiming for a world record; you just need to be aiming for *better*.

It is specifically designed for self-directed learners. If you do not have a coach standing over your shoulder correcting your form, you need to learn to be your own coach. You need to learn how to diagnose your own bottlenecks, generate your own feedback loops, and structure your own curriculum.

## What you will find inside

This is not a theoretical treatise on neuroscience, though we will touch on how the brain processes information. It is a manual for action. Specifically, this guide covers:

- **The mechanics of working memory:** Understanding why you get overwhelmed and how building "mental representations" (chunks) is the only way to bypass biological limits.
- **Task alignment:** Why you are likely practicing the wrong thing (like practicing "recognition" when you actually need "recall") and how to fix your posture.
- **Concrete techniques:** Seven specific methods to vary your repetition, including back-chaining, speed variation, and artificial constraints.
- **The emotional grind:** An honest discussion about the boredom and frustration of practice, and strategies to manage the emotional weight of learning.

My goal is to move you from "mindless repetition" to "reflective practice." By the end of this guide, you will have a personal roadmap to break through your current limits and achieve fluency.

sections.title: Working Memory Limitations
sections.content:
# Working Memory and How to Overcome Its Limitations Through Practice

## Summary of key facts about working memory

1. Working memory is what we can keep active in the mind while we perform mental operations.
2. There are only a limited number of chunks of information we can keep in working memory at one time (between 4 and 10). When new ones are added, old ones are pushed out.
3. The size of the chunks is not limited. In fact, sometimes making them bigger makes it easier, particularly, if we increase their size by making them more meaningful to us.

## What is working memory and why it matters for good performance

Working memory is the small mental buffer you use to keep things on top of mind so that you can do something with them. You need working memory when you do mental calculations, compare ideas, recognise faces, drive a car, or when you write a sentence. Without it, we would be too slow at doing any of these things.

There are many things we don’t know for certain about working memory but we are sure, it is very limited. It can only hold about 7 discrete items at once (some people say it’s even less but definitely no more than 10). 

A good simple example is writing down a phone number someone is dictating to you. Unless you focus, you can usually only do it a few digits at a time and nobody can do a whole 10 digit phone number. Just remembering each digit individually and then writing them down one by one is impossible without some mental tricks. And it’s these sort of tricks that we can learn from.

The very simplest mental trick is to chunk the numbers. So instead of putting **2 3 5 6 7 8 9  1 9 3 6** into your working memory buffer one by one, you can do **2356 7789 1936**. Now you only have three chunks in working memory. This is easier but the chunks don’t mean anything, so it will still be a challenge. So instead, you can decide to chunk the numbers in a way that has some meaning. **23** (how old your cousin is) **5677** (a house number) **89** (number of a road you travel on) **1936** (date in history). All of a sudden, it’s much easier to quickly put the numbers into your working memory and keep them there. (The world record holder can use this approach to memorise 514 digits in 5 minutes.)

So what we did was:

1. Create chunks
2. Make the chunks bigger and richer by adding meaning

This seems like a paradox. If working memory is limited, how can we make it easier to think when we put more in? That is the second thing we are sure about when it comes to working memory. Even though the number of chunks we can keep in it is limited, the size of the chunks is not. Chunks, by the way, is the technical term in the research, so we will use this here, as well. 

## Working memory in practice

How does this work in practice? We use working memory for much more than just writing down phone numbers. It is involved in everything we do. Working memory is fundamental to speaking, reading and writing. Here is another example. Take this English sentence:

> Books are often very expensive.
> 

It probably took you less than a second to read and understand. (Assuming you are a native speaker who does not have dyslexia or some other difficulty that slows down processing.)

Let’s take a similar sentence in another language. Let’s say Czech. You probably don’t speak Czech but, it should be very easy to translate, if I give you all the words first.

Here is an alphabetical list of the four words that will appear in the sentence.

| jsou | are |
| --- | --- |
| knihy | books |
| staré | old |
| támhle | over there |

Now, how long does it take you to read and understand this sentence?

> Staré knihy jsou támhle.
> 

Probably at least 10 seconds. Why? You have to look up every single word in the list and then put them together in your mind. But all those words are unfamiliar and they take up a lot of space in your working memory. So it is possible that even after you put them all together you have no mental capacity to do anything else with that sentence. Such as make it into a question by swapping the verb and the subject. It is very simple:

> Jsou staré knihy támhle?
> 

But you probably couldn’t do it without a lot of effort. What are some strategies you could use to translate and transform the sentence. There are essentially three:

(1) First, you would probably want to remove everything else that may be taking up space in your working memory. This means focusing just on the sentence. Removing visual distractions such as not looking anywhere else, minimising other audio input such as turning down music, remove thoughts of other things by trying to focus on just the task at hand.

(2) Second, you would want to offload some of the load from your working memory somewhere else. The best way to do that is to write down each individual word as you translate it on a piece of paper. And when I ask you to switch the subject and verb, you may want to circle the two words that constitute the subject (old books) and underline the verb (jsou).

But none of these methods are sustainable in the long term. You could not translate very many sentences doing this. And you would never be able to have a conversation in the language. Looking up every word of a sentence in a dictionary is not how you speak, read or write a language. So this leads us to the next strategy that lies at the heart of this programme.

(3) Third, combine the words into meaningful chunks in your mind. You could try to find some surface similarities to create a mnemonic devices. For example, *staré* sounds kind of like *starry* and you could associate *knihy* with *knights* who go *high*. But this is very hard to do quickly and only works for recalling the words, not doing something with them.

(4) So you are left with the only other option and that is to practice the language. This would involve repeating different combinations of words many times to create chunks that you can use in working memory. But it would also require that you think about how the words are put together and also about the ways of trying to learn them. And, most importantly, you would need to make sure that what you are saying has real meaning to you.

This has been called **deliberate practice** and it lies at the heart of the Writing Boot Up. Deliberate practice is like any other practice. You repeat actions until you can perform them with ease. But the core of deliberate practice is that this repetition involves focus and reflection. And these are aimed explicitly at helping you overcome the limitations of working memory by developing ‘bigger chunks’  and storing them for later use as mental representations.

## Reflective repetition as a way of overcoming working memory limitations and performance plateaus

To get better at anything, we need to practice. We cannot just think about how to do something, we have to try it first. And usually we have to repeat it many times before we get better at it. Just think about how long it took you to learn to drive. There are many steps to just getting started and simply thinking about them is not enough. You have to practice in small chunks and slowly it becomes easy. 

But very soon, we stop getting better no matter how many times we repeat something. This means we reach a plateau. To break through a plateau, we need to reflect on what it is that we’re doing, what gets in the way and what else we could try to improve with the next round of repetitions. As we reach close to the limit of what is possible, more reflection and more focused repetition is needed. As you get closer to being the best you can be, you may have to do a lot of this for relatively small gains. But initially, adding reflection to repetition can help us make great strides.

To summarise the key principle behind this approach, we can say:

<aside>
💡 **Repetition** without reflection leads to **performance plateaus**. 
**Reflection** without repetition leads to **paralysis in action**.

</aside>

We get better at many things after doing them a few times. But after a while we stop improving. So we have to be more focused on how we repeat things. It is best if what we are trying to learn has a nice programme of step by step improvement we can follow such as Couch to 5K. But if there is not one, you can still improve by focusing on what you are practicing.

The key principle behind our reflection should be:

<aside>
💡 Is what I’m repeating (and the way I’m repeating it) helping me overcome the limits of working memory by building richer and more useful mental representation that I can work with as chunks in the working memory?

</aside>

sections.title: Fluency as Target
sections.content:
# Fluency as the Target of Practice

## Why you should target fluency in practice

Being able to keep more in working memory is essential to fluent and accurate performance. Accuracy is self-evident but people rarely think about fluency. Fluency means that you can perform the action quickly enough not to get stuck and loose track of what you’re trying to do. 

We most often talk about fluency when it comes to speaking a language. When we say ‘She is fluent in Swahili’ we mean that she can have a conversation with someone without constantly stopping and thinking about how to say something. Everybody who’s tried to learn a second language knows what it feels like when you don’t have enough fluency. You feel like a fool because you can never say what you want when you most need it.

But fluency is very important to any performance.  Whether it is speaking, writing, reading, playing a musical instrument, driving or even editing, you need to be able to do it quickly enough to get where you are going.

<aside>
💡 When you practice, your aim should be to develop fluency first and accuracy second.

</aside>

## Lessons from dyslexia about the importance of fluency

One of the more well-known learning difficulties that causes problems with reading and writing is dyslexia. This is often thought about as misspelling words. But most people do not realise that by far the biggest impact of dyslexia is on fluency.  

In fact, dyslexia is defined as a phonological processing limitation that causes problems with “fluent and accurate reading and writing”. What this means is that a dyslexic reader or writer will be so slow in decoding individual words that by the time they get to the end of the sentence, they don’t know what it’s about. And working memory deficit is one of the most common issues people with dyslexia face. 

Dyslexia is a neurological feature but even people without dyslexia feel similar effects when they are in a situation when their working memory is put under stress. In other words, their ability to write or read fluently is diminished and often their accuracy suffers, as well. There are many things that put stress on your working memory but  speaking or reading in a foreign language would come top of the list. And for most people ‘academic writing’ often feels like a foreign language.

## Fluency vs unconscious competence

It would be a mistake to think of fluent performance as not having to think about what we’re doing. Many people have heard of the four stages of competence model ([Four stages of competence model](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Four_stages_of_competence)) in which you progress through these four stages when developing any skill:

1. Unconscious incompetence: Not knowing we can’t do something
2. Conscious incompetence: Realising we can’t do something
3. Conscious competence: Becoming aware of being able to do something
4. Unconscious competence: Doing something without thinking

This is a useful guide to thinking about the process of learning but there is a great danger of misinterpreting the final stage as being ‘so good at something’ we can do it without thinking about it. In fact, the original author warned against this very stage as being a symptom that people will stop improving.

The final stage of competence will feel like you can do something without paying conscious attention but that’s only because your working memory is not being constantly swamped. But the aim should not be to be able to do something without thinking but to but to be able to do it because we can think with bigger chunks.

The chunks in your working memory are not closed off blocks, they have internal structure and being able to bring this structure out is essential when encountering a new situation or when something goes wrong. An expert performer must not only be able to something but also to notice problems and recover from them. A musician may play a wrong note, an actor may have to respond to a disruption from the audience, a driver may have to deal with a non-responsive break. Dealing with all of those situations requires being able to take apart and recombine the chunks at high speed. 

This is extremely relevant to academic writing because it is important for a writer to not just string together chunks academic-sounding language but also to say something with it. In fact, academic writers have to paraphrase what others are saying. They also have to be able to edit what they wrote which again requires conscious attention. Writing requires thinking, but thinking fluently.

This is why practice also requires thinking, focus and reflection. Which brings us to the next section.

<aside>
💡 Expertise is never unconscious. Being an expert does not mean acting without thinking, it means thinking with bigger more complex chunks while acting.

</aside>

sections.title: Schemas & Chunks
sections.content:
# Schemas and chunks: What needs to go in your memory

## What you actually need to “remember”

Contrary to the impression you may get if you read popular books by cognitive psychologists, we know almost nothing about memory. We know quite a few things about what happens when people try to remember and how they forget, but exactly what happens in the brain when people try to memorise something is a complete mystery. 

The most common way in which most people think about memory is as some sort of storage into which you reach with your mind and retrieve what you are looking for. But the truth is, we just don’t know if that is what memory is like. There are some aspects of memory that behave like storage, but there are others that are very different.

Pretty much everything that we say about memory is some kind of metaphor. Metaphors can be incredibly useful but we should be careful about drawing inferences from them. Here, I will use the metaphor of an inventory of mental schemas from which we retrieve chunks onto a sort of mental shelf where we can combine them into a useful product. But that is all it is - a metaphor.

The storage metaphor breaks down very often. Memory simply does not seem to behave like a storage of objects in many ways. For example, It does not seem to run out of space in a straightforward way. The more we put in, and the more we make connections between what we had placed there, the more seems to be able to fit in. Also, we can often retrieve things from the back of this metaphorical storage more easily than from the front. That is not how storage spaces work in the literal sense. So we must be incredibly careful about what we say when it’s time for things like long-term and short-term memory.

## Mental representations or embodied mental schemas

While we know very little about the exact nature of memory, we know even less about what is actually stored in there. We do know what the things that come out look like: Words, memories, ideas, images,  episodes, etc. But it is pretty unlikely, they are just stored somewhere in a neuron in a brain for us to retrieve. We wouldn’t know where to start finding the boundaries.

The problem with memory as storage is that we have no easy way to explain how those memories get into working memory. And we also do not know how the sort of practice we do, would put them in the storage in a way that is actually useful when we need them. What sort of things am I pulling out of my head as I am writing this sentence? What did it take for me to put them there? English is not my first language, so it took a long time to learn all the structures, but I also had to learn to type fast enough to do it, the rules of spelling and so on. Individually, it is a long list of things, yet, they seemingly just happen. We do not have a very good theory of what is happening here other than just waving a hand to say that we’re retrieving items.

One way of resolving this problem is thinking about what is in our brain as an inventory of embodied mental schemas. This may seem like an unnecessary diversion but it is actually important as we contemplate what we practice and why. But feel free to skip this section. 

We need to answer three questions:

1. Why schemas instead of simple units
2. Why embodied instead of just plain concepts
3. Why an inventory instead of some structured storage 

### Why schemas

We tend to think that the words in our head are very simple. But they are not - they come with a lot of underlying knowledge. Adjectives are a useful example. We take the colour green. When I something important is happening when I say ‘green leaf’ or a ‘green car’. When I tear apart a leaf, I expect to still see the colour green. Yet, when I open the door of a green car, I expect to see no green at all. Green cars are green on the outside, leaves all the way through. To combine the colour green with the word car is very different from combining it with the word leaf. 

What comes into play is our knowledge of the world. Leaves are green through and through, and cars are green only when painted. This is just one tiny thing about leaves and cars, yet, it would take pages to adequately describe it. But we understand both instantly and make the right inferences. So, a good way of thinking about this is as having relatively schematic outlines of things in our head that we can then use instantly but fitting multiple ones together into one.

The same goes for nouns, verbs and other things. All books are different but I don’t have a problem recognising all of them as book. Everybody runs differently (people, animals), yet I can immediately recognise something as running. So, what is in my head doesn’t make sense as a perfect picture, it is some sort of an outline. 

Even grammar rules are such outlines. I don’t have a rule in my head that tells me Noun + Verb make a sentence (a dog runs). I have a schema that may look something like this: [[nouny thing][verby things]]. These schemas can get quite large but it seems we are able to use them. (There is a whole theory behind this called construction or cognitive grammar, but that is not too relevant, here.)

This is very useful because, when I practice, my aim is to create ever larger schemas that I can instantaneously combine as I perform. It makes no sense to develop structures that are too specific.  

Let’s take this joke by the Comedian Mitch Hedberg: “I like escalators. They never break. They just become stairs.” What sort of information would you have to have stored in your head, how would you retrieve it, and combine it to understand this joke? You could perhaps come up with a way to explain one such joke. But there are thousands like this in English alone. In some way it is easier to imagine that we have schemas that we simply overlay on top of one another and a new image emerges. Like to prints on semi transparent paper.

Calling up such schemas and overlaying them on top of one another is what chunking inside working memory is. Or at least, it is a useful way to think about it that way. We actually have no idea how it happens in practice. If, instead, we think of this as computing some sort of sequence of instructions, we run into the problem is that that is what working memory is for. But we need something to present to working memory - and those are chunks composed out of embodied mental schemas.

### Why embodied

Why not just talk about concepts we have in our head? Ericsson calls these things mental representations. But these things are neither pure representations nor purely mental. When we learn things, we involve our bodies in all sorts of ways.

Our bodies give us the basic framework for understanding spatial relations and all the other concepts derived from them like: inside, excluded, overarching, etc. 

But that’s not really what matters here. What is really important is that most of the things we are learning with deliberate practice have a bodily component. When we write, we use our fingers and hands. But also our backs and our backsides. We experience tiredness, we occupy the space around us, we hear noises, etc. All of those are also involved in reading. When we learn a foreign language, we gesture, move our mouths, etc.

Of course, some skills require less action with our bodies than others. Running or lifting weights is mostly a matter of the body (although surprisingly also a very mental exercise) and chess a lot less (although surprisingly it has a bodily component). Some other less physical disciplines still require a of bodily involvement. Music is very much a bodily exercise.

Even seemingly purely mental skills like doing maths have this bodily component.  Doing mathematics cannot be done without putting things on paper, standing around whiteboards, etc. Both chess and maths can be done in the head only but only up to a point and only after involving the body for a long time.

And we do know that when we practice, to develop these skills, we have to involve the body. So, it makes sense to assume that they are a part of the schemas. And we can improve how useful they are to us if we incorporate our bodies into them even more.

We can think of the embodied schemas as the sort of gestures we perform to solve normal problems. When we feel a mosquito on our face, we automatically touch the spot with out hand. It is an incredibly complicated gesture, but we do it automatically.  Our aim is to develop such mental schemas that they start to feel to us as easy and natural as touch a spot on our face.

### Why inventory

These schemas are not all alike. They vary in richness, some are static, some are dynamic, some are extremely specific and others very general. It is not clear how many we have and how many we need. But if we tried to make a list, we’d probably end up with millions. This sounds extreme but that is what Psyc project found when they tried to document knowledge in a way that would represent it to a computer. 

So the question is, how do we keep them all in our head and in our bodies? The short answer is, we don’t know. But a good way is to think of them as an inventory of good available for sale in a large supermarket. There is no definite best way in which they are organised, their place changes based on the time of day or customer demand, some are more and some are less readily accessible. 

We are constantly replenishing and refreshing that inventory but ultimately we have to spend money, effort, time and resources to keep it full and organised. What it is not is a box where we simply put one thing after another.

Of course, in some ways it is more like a giant warehouse than an inventory, we cannot see it all at once and sometimes things get lost, they fade or expire beyond usefulness.

And in some ways it is like neither of these things. There are no practical limits on how much we seem to be able to store and it is almost as easy to get to things at the back as it is at the front. 

But nevertheless, it is useful to use a metaphor like inventory to help us.

## More about chunks and mental representations

Fluent performance breaks down when the limits of working memory are reached. We can think of the limits roughly as a fixed number of chunks of information. And the only way to overcome the limit in the moment is to chunk information together into bigger chunks because there does not seem to be a limit on the size or richness of those chunks. 

We know that it takes reflective and purposeful practice to develop the ability to work with these chunks. But a big question remains. What are the chunks like and where are they stored? The short answer is we don’t know. But one way to think about them (inspired by Anders Ericsson) is as ‘mental representations’. 

Unfortunately, Ericsson or other researchers have not really had much to say about the nature of these representations. We just know something like them exists because we know when people focus on them, their performance improves. So provisionally, we can think of them as some structures in the mind that are available to working memory without any retrieval effort (look and know knowledge). This makes them different from more encyclopaedic knowledge we often have to work hard to retrieve from memory.

Mental representations is an unfortunate term for two reasons:

1. It implies that they are concepts to be learned about whereas they are structures to acquire through practice.
2. It implies that only ‘mind’ things are involved whereas these representations are really embodied. We can think of them perhaps even better as mental gestures.

But we need a term to distinguish between the chunks that we use during performance. And the long-term structures that we are developing through practice. The reason for this is that we can also create ad-hoc chunks (such as when remembering a phone number) which is different from the chunks we develop through practice.

## What do ‘mental representations look like’?

We must not confuse mental representations with analytic categories. Analytic categories are the domain of conceptual learning. But mental representations are essential for procedural learning. And paradoxically, they are not always the same. With analytic categories, our aim is to have an accurate understanding of something, with mental representations, we are looking to develop fluent performance. 

We can best illustrate it on the difference between knowing about the grammar of a language and knowing how to speak a language. Native speakers have no problem constructing complex sentences at fluent conversational speed but when you ask them how those sentences are put together, they usually give an answer that is different from that of a grammarian.

They are able to speak fluently by recombining chunks of language, rather than putting individual words together according to the rules of grammar. And these chunks are often very different from the categories found in a grammar book. For example, beginner readers often benefit from decomposing longer words into their parts. They learn that ‘teacher’ is the result of putting together ‘teach’ and “-er”.  This makes it easier to read and write. But they may also use that same principle to learn how to read the word ‘corner’, even though ‘corner’ is not the result of putting together ‘corn’ + ‘-er’.

Mental representations that we develop to assist in fluent performance are often different from the conceptual representations of the same thing. Sometimes this is a small idiosyncrasy of the individual, but sometimes it is a necessary stage of development. Complete beginners in any field are often taught through great oversimplification.

This has important implications for learning. 

1. It is not always necessary to start ‘at the bottom’ of a conceptual hierarchy.
2. It is not always necessary to learn ‘all the basics’ first.

For example, it is possible to learn read or write a language without learning to speak it first. You may need some basics of pronunciation to make it easier to sound out words, but you don’ have to take a whole conversational course. And equally, it is possible to learn to write an academic paper before learning to write a letter to a friend. 

Our practice should be aimed at the demands of the task we are trying to develop fluency in, not at being able to replicate how the task is described in theory.  And it may not always be immediately obvious what the demands of the task are or even what the task itself is. 

For example, many people use gamified apps for language learning. They are motivated by rewards, positions on leaderboards, competition with friends. But this means that the task they end up practicing is succeeding at the game. They optimise their mental representations towards that task and become very good at it. But this very often does not translate into being able to speak.

Unless the practice is always closely linked to actual performance, success in practice will deceive us into thinking that we are improving at the thing we are trying to practice. We are improving but at the wrong task. We are getting better at succeeding in the practice task and that success may have very different needs than succeeding at the real task. 

That’s why, it is essential that we get real feedback from real situations as soon as possible. We need to link the components we are practicing in with the larger context of performance. Often, ‘actually doing it’ may be the only solution. Athletes often perform better on courses where they had competed before. But this is not realistic in most situations, which is why visualisation or even verbal rehearsal is such an important part of practice.

In other words, dealing with the environment is a part of the task which is why it is important to practice in the context of performance. Practicing for an exam is best done under exam conditions. Practicing for a musical performance is best done with an audience. And so on. 

There is a joke about a jazz musician who was approached by a fan after a great performance. The fan was shocked when they saw the musician was drunk. “How were you able to play so well when you’re drunk”, the fan asked. “Well, that’s because I practice drunk.” replied the musician. The lesson here is not about alcohol but about the importance of practicing for the actual task required for fluent performance.

sections.title: Two Kinds of Memory
sections.content:
# Two kinds of memory and two kinds of retrieval

## Two kinds of memory or knowledge

People talk about two kinds of learning or even two kinds of knowledge:

1. **Conceptual knowledge:** understanding definitions, concepts, rules, or principles
2. **Procedural knowledge:** being able to perform activities such as solving a math equation, applying the right grammar rule in the correct context

You can acquire conceptual knowledge by reading, listening to lectures and then thinking about it or even better discussing it with colleagues. With simple enough concepts, you can even learn something conceptually in a few minutes.

But procedural knowledge can only be acquired through practice and over time. It is relatively easy to learn a list of words and a few rules for using them. But when you try to actually say a sentence in a real context, that kind of knowledge seems completely out of reach. Your working memory simply is not big enough to retrieve the words, put endings on them and put them in the right order while also thinking about what you want to say or worrying about what the other person thinks of your accent.

The biggest mistake people make is to assume that just because they understand some concept, they can use it in actual performance. In general, people almost always practice too little and learn the rules too much. They value understanding over the ability to do something with that understanding. 

And things get even worse. That is because conceptual knowledge actually relies on procedural knowledge. As the concepts get more complicated, it becomes more difficult to just keep all aspects of the ideas in your head. We learn concepts to do something with them. But if we can’t hold enough of the concept in our working memory at the same time as another one, even a simple thing like comparison is out of reach.

So it is worthwhile to insert little moments of practice even into conceptual learning. Particularly when encountering one of these:

- Abstract concepts
- Acronyms
- Terms, foreign words, names
- Equations
- Variables
- Functions

| Conceptual | Procedural |
| --- | --- |
| 1. Developing mental maps of the area of competence
2. Is developed through engagement with content such as guides, lessons, etc. | 1. Developing fluency of performance in the area of competence
2. Relies on ability to perceive and act based on the perception
3. Is developed through a feedback loop of repetition and reflection |

## Two kinds of retrieval: “Look and know” vs “Look up and know”

When we talk about conceptual or procedural knowledge, we always think of it as something that is stored somewhere in your brain or in our muscles (or a combination of both). But the actual question that is of interest to us here is how we retrieve those pieces of knowledge from this storage into working memory.

From this perspective we can differentiate between two types of memory retrieval based on the way we get its contents from wherever it is stored in a dormant state into our working memory where we can do something with it.  They are:

1. Look and know
2. Look up and know

### Look and know retrieval

**Look and know retrieval of knowledge** (or skill) is at the very foundation of our existence. As you go through the world, you look at things and you immediately know what they are. Objects, people’s faces, words you see or hear. When you need them, they just appear in your working memory for you to be able to think with them. They are almost integrated into your body. You want to pick up an object and you reach out and take it. You want to say a sentence about it and you just do it. 

### Look up and know retrieval

**Look up and know** is the kind of knowledge (or skill) retrieval that requires effort to make knowledge available for thinking with. It is like looking up a word in a dictionary before you say it. And that process takes time and mental energy which takes up a space in your working memory. You can do fewer things with knowledge that you have to look up before you can do something with it.

These two types are similar but not exactly the same as the conceptual vs procedural distinction. 

## Table comparing different types of knowledge and retrieval

| **** | **Conceptual:**  Look up and know | **Procedural:**  Look and know |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Ease of retrieval into working memory | Needs to be retrieved from long-term storage. | Is immediately available for cognitive operations. |
| **Cognitive demands** | ·  High demand on working memory.
· Can only be retrieved one step at a time.
·  Limited ability to use for complex mental or physical operations. | ·  Low demand on working memory.
·  Can be retrieved instantaneously.
·  Can be used for complex mental or physical operations. |
| **Practical implications** | Not useful for fluent performance in most tasks with any level of complexity. | Necessary for performance but limited use for developing overall understanding. |
| **Examples** | · Recognise unfamiliar face
· Remember a word to fill in a blank
· Remember a mathematical formula | · Recognise familiar faces
· Use a word in conversation
· Use a formula to produce a result |
| **Disciplines that primarily rely on** | · History
· Grammar
· Philosophy
· Music theory
· Medical knowledge
· Computer science
· Set theory | · Speaking a language
· Coding
· Mathematics
· Engineering
· Musical performance
· Diagnostic medicine
· Surgery |
| **Acquisition** | Through engagement with content. | Through purposeful practice based on reflective repetition. |

sections.title: Key Points on Memory
sections.content:
# Key points about mental representations and working memory

<aside>
💡 You do not need to know how to walk before you can run. But you may need to learn how to walk eventually.

</aside>

- The number of chunks that can be in our working memory at any one time is limited. We are not exactly sure what the exact limit is but we know there is one and that it is more less the same across the population. There is nobody with an ‘order of magnitude’ larger working memory capacity.
- There is no limit to the size of the chunks in working memory; in fact, the richer in meaning they are, the better. This is a metaphor. We do not know exactly what those chunks look like and exactly how they work. But we know enough about how people use them to be able to make this a working assumption.
- The chunks exist in our skills inventory as mental representations (I am purposely not calling this long term memory because I do not want to pollute the concept with questions of storage or form; I also do not want to limit this to something that is purely in the ‘brain’)
- Mental representations does NOT mean concepts or ideas because they may contain physical components - we can just as easily think of them as gestures.
- We can acquire mental representations through repetition and we can increase their complexity through reflective repetition. We do not know exactly how much repetition is required but we know there’s a limit to the utility of unreflective repetition.
- For certain types of knowledge or skill performance requiring a high degree of fluency for basic successl, purposeful or deliberate practice is require to develop mental representations that are amenable to chunking into working memory.
- Mental representations are not ‘monadic’ or ‘objects with clear boundaries’ - they are not black boxes to us (up to a point) and we can access their components
- **Most importantly** mental representations do not have to (and usually do not) correspond to real categories or components as identified in textbooks. For example, if thinking or ‘corner’ as being ‘corn+er’ the same way as ‘teacher’ is ‘teach+er’ is wrong at the level of linguistic description but if somebody can use it to make it easier to learn to spell ‘corner’ (as some people do), that is a perfectly fine mental representation.

sections.title: Practice for Performance
sections.content:
# Practice for Performance

## The three tasks of performance and targets of practice

When we practice, we say that we do it to learn things. But since the target of practice is procedural performance rather than conceptual knowledge, we need to be very clear about what it is that we are trying to develop. 

## **Three components of performance**

Any performance consists of three components or inputs. They all play a different role, require different schemas and different practice. Yet, they feed into each other. Each of the components can be thought of independently but usually they are very interconnected. Different disciplines and tasks with them differ in how prominent these components are within them.

The three components are: 

1. Mental map
2. Perceptive eye
3. Fluent muscle

### **Mental maps**

Mental map is what allows you to orient yourself in the situation you are facing. It is your primary sense-making instrument - it governs what you focus on, what you ignore and how you solve problems or react to new situations. Sometimes they are referred to as mental model.

The mental map or model are not the same as concepts about what you are facing. They are entirely pragmatic to help you achieve what you want. Just like any maps, they are not the territory. They can be extremely simplified or even slightly wrong but they are still useful.

For example, the mental map of a situation of you reading in a room with an open window and hearing a noise outside. Your mental map tells you that the hole in the wall is letting more sound in, so you stand up and close the window. 

Another example is that you come to a device with a display or with a chord leading to an electrical outlet. Your mental map tells you that such devices have ways of being turned on, so you will look for a switch.

Mental maps also help you solve problems. The mental map you have of books is that they have sequential pages and text that ends on one continues on another. When the text going from one page to next stops making sense, you will check the page number to see if somebody tore out a page.

When you are writing and you cannot think of the next word, your mental map will send you to the thesaurus and will tell you roughly where to look.

To develop mental maps, you have to combine conceptual and procedural learning. Mental maps are not ideas or definitions. They are models of the problems you are trying to solve or the task you are trying to accomplish.

### **Perceptive eye**

Simply having a map to guide you is not enough, if you cannot recognise waypoints or that you have achieved your destination. That’s why you also need an eye that can perceive what your map is orienting you towards.

Your eye can recognise multiple features of a device your map tells you can be turned on as a button. 

When reading or writing, you have to be able to recognise the words and sentences as being about the thing you are writing - not just some drops of ink on a page. When speaking a language, you have to be able to hear the words as words and not just as a series of noises.

This may sound trivial because these are examples of things with which you are intimately familiar. But just try doing these things with a new language or a new device and you will soon experience what it is like to have a mental map without a perceptive eye.

You must be able to recognise things as examples of the things you have developed mental maps for. You may have a mental map that tells you to write in an academic style but that is not helpful if you cannot recognise what academic style looks like.

To develop a perceptive eye, you have to experience a lot of examples with feedback.

### **Fluent muscle**

Finally, in order to be able to achieve anything, you have to develop fluency. You have to be able to perform the task quickly enough so that it does not just dissolve into meaningless components.

The fluency very often has some bodily dimension. Writing, speaking, playing chess, playing a piano, catching a ball - all of those require some involvement of the body as part of the activity. Without fluency, the performance would be so halting as to be useless or even stop being what we intend. Playing one note and waiting 10 seconds while we remember how to play the next one is no longer playing a song.

But even in less bodily activities such as reading or doing mathematics, we still require fluency. In fact, we can think of those activities quite usefully as sort of gestures. Postures we adopt as we orient our mind towards a problem. There’s always some muscle and movement involved - turning the page, moving our head to look at a graph, positioning the page to better see it. And it would be a mistake to ignore these. They are a part of the gesture.

As we know, fluency is where working memory plays the most important role because if we overload the buffer, we stop being able to do things at a minimum speed and the performance breaks down. This happens very quickly, sometimes so quickly that we may not even bother getting started. 

So, we could say that developing fluent muscle is what is needed just to get started. You don’t start playing a song until you have played the individual notes at some sort of speed with the required gaps between them. You don’t really start speaking until you’ve said a sentence and you don’t start writing until you can write a sentence (or at least a sentence-like pattern) at a time.

But it is important to remember that fluent muscle is just a metaphor for fluency. It does not have to be muscle what is involved. But it is something we can develop.

## **Disciplines and the muscle / mental map / perceptive eye balance**

Different discicplines will have a different balance of emphasis as to the elements of performance. History is very heavily focused towards the mental map balance whereas playing baseball is much more about the fluency of physical movement. But even historians have to have perceptive eyes to recognise archival documents quickly enough as relevant and fluent muscles so that they can write about it.

Perhaps the most balanced of all disciplines is musical performance. A musician has to have a finely attuned ear so that they can tell what they are hearing is good enough and they have to have quite sophisticated mental maps of the music they are playing. But above all, they require a huge amount of fluency which they spend thousands of hours developing through deliberate practice and constantly honing and maintaining. 

> A musician says: if I don’t practice for a day God knows, if I don’t practice for two days, I know and if I don’t practice for three days, the audience knows. [ref]
> 

Chess is a bit different from music because the fluency does not have to be as embodied and in some matches, it is less important. But in blitz Chess, the fluency of performance is essential.

Writing is in many ways somewhere between music and chess. Unlike music, we don’t have the need to peform without stopping to think but we do have to be able to compose in sufficiently large chunks to get anything done. If we wrote at the speed of chess moves, nothing would ever get written. But writing has more space for developing mental maps and perceptive eye. We have to be able to recognise different types of writing.

## **Three metaphors of how schemas get from inventory to working memory**

So, now we have established two crucial facts about performance:

1. In order to perform most tasks at a higher level, we need to operate with larger chunks in our working memory
2. To perform better, we need to practice to build up an inventory of embodied mental schemas

We can be fairly confident that this is a sufficient requirement to develop a successful programme of practice that will lead to better performance. We have examples of successful programmes that use one or both of these facts as a working assumption. But it would be very helpful for thinking about how to make the most out of these, if we had a good working theory of how we get the embodied schemas from their inventory to working memory and combine them to perform sophisticated and fluent actions.

The simple answer is we do not know. But we can come up with some useful metaphors that will help us in thinking about it and making some useful adjustments to our programme of practice. The metaphors are:

1. Computation
2. Projected overlays
3. Clay impressions

### **Computational metaphor**

I claimed that we do not know how the contents of our minds get pulled into working memory where we can use them for performance. But many people will claim we do. They are most likely to be using a version of the computational metaphor of the mind.

Many people may not have a good model of computation. The easiest way to think about it is as a series of if-then statements. If the I move my pawn to this square, my opponent will be able to take it with her rook. If the shape I’m seeing in front of me is standing on two feet, has a head with hair on top but none on their torso, I’m looking at a human being. And so on.

This is a very seductive metaphor because everybody has experienced that kind of a process in their head when they are trying to make a decision. But it is not actually very useful for learning. That is because we cannot describe all the things that need to happen computationally in this way. There are just too many computations.

In the sentence about recognising human beings, I used a lot of words. But they would also have to be computed. How do I know that what I’m seeing is a head and what I’m seeing on top of this is hair? Every single thing would have to be computed. And computations need operations like is, not, if, then and they need to work on things with clear boundaries. This works for chess boards but not much else - we also have to assume that the inputs into our computation exist as solid objects - and that is not very helpful when we try to figure our how to learn to perform quickly. Because we know that we are not explicitly making if-then statements when we recognise what we see.

Maybe our brain is doing it at some level but not at the level accessible to us - and not in a way that would be useful to performance. In fact, it would actively harm performance. So whether, the computational metaphor is useful to cognitive science or artificial intelligence or not, it is not useful for helping us think about learning to get better at performance. 

For that, we can use the metaphor or a transparent overlays which is inspired by the conceptual metaphor theory which provides a sense of what schemas look like and its successor conceptual integration theory which helps us think about how we reason with them [ref - Lakoff 1987, Fauconnier and Turner 2003].

### **Projected overlays**

Imagine two semi-transparent sheets of paper (lets’ call them transparencies). These transparencies have various images drawn on them. Some are very detailed, others just outline sketches, some full of colour, others in black and white, some very sharp and others fuzzy. When you put two or more such sheets together and hold them up against the light, new shapes appear. Some elements of some shapes may get new outlines, others may be hidden, yet others filled in. What happens depends on how well we aligned the sheets, their orientation and also the order in which we put them together. 

We can put as many sheets together if we like but there are limits to what can be used. Too many, and previously newly emerged shapes disappear again or are transformed. And eventually light stops shining through. 

What is important about this metaphor is that we have a very good bodily depiction of this that anybody can experience. And what we know from that experience is that the new image that comes out of the combination is instantaneous. It does not require a computation. In fact, we would find it difficult to compose a series of if-then statements that would give us that outcome.

This in fact describes how most people go about their life. They quickly pull up schemas and overlay them on top of one another to get new results. Because these overlays are never perfectly aligned, we experience new and unexpected shapes - which gives us creativity, something that is really difficult to capture under the purely computational metaphor.

But it is not exactly true that no computation is involved. When we are trying to go further, we may make some of these statements about the how we position the sheets and what would happened if we did that. That’s what it feels like when we reason. But notice, we are reasoning about the positioning of the overlays (concepts, schemas), not about their contents. Those just come up.

This is a very useful metaphor for thinking about using and combining mental schemas. But it lacks any notion of learning or return feedback. These are crucial for thinking about practice. So, this is where the clay metaphor comes in.

### **Clay impressions**

Imagine a ground covered with clay from which you want to make shapes using molds and cookie cutters. But the clay is not uniform, it reaches deeper in some places and hides rocks in others. It also contains ruts and grooves from previous cuttings. So, when we try to impress our molds or cutters into it, sometimes they go too deep and other times they can’t get in. Or can’t get in uniformly.

This means that sometimes we have to push harder or multiple times and sometimes we may even need a hammer to press the cutters in. Or sometimes, we need to reorient these molds so that they fit around the obstacles. Some of this happens without thinking and some of it requires that we pause and think about what might be hiding under the mud.

To get the shapes we want, we have to use our bodies and our minds, employ both automatic and deliberative actions, repeat the same action multiple times and then change our approach when it is not working. As the consistency of the clay changes, we react to the changes by slow adjustments in pressure. But we may also bring different tools as we want to create more elaborate shapes.

The clay metaphor is useful for thinking about how we develop the schemas we have in our inventory as we interact with our environment. It is not a matter of collecting things that just lie out there and that we can pick up and stack up somewhere. We are actively engaged in their creation. We leave an impression in the world and in return in makes an impression in us. 

We have all experienced physical activities like that as children or as adults. But we think of them as separate from the work of thinking and learning. But in fact, thinking and learning is much more like this than it is like a computer. So, as we try to develop our inventory of mental representations we should not be afraid to push against the subject or our discipline, feel the touch of it and adjust our reaction. This will not be nearly as instantaneous as when we push a mold into clay, it the principle is the same.

sections.title: Avoiding Task Misalignment
sections.content:
# Avoiding Task Misalignment for Successful Practice

## Task alignment and posture

When you perform some action, your body and/or you mind are performing a task. You are deploying all the resources to accomplish that task. Your entire being orients itself towards the accomplishment. If you can actually perform the task with any level of fluency, all of this happens automatically. When you speak, your mouth opens and makes the right shapes, when you walk, your body changes posture, when you read, your eyes focus and your brain is attuned to perceiving ink blots on a page as meaningful.

### **Running pose example**

In some ways, you only know what the task is from the posture you adopt. A good example is demonstrating running. When you are asked to adopt a static pose of a runner, you will most likely stand on one foot, lean forward, step out with the other foot and put your arm forward. Most people (as online photos show) put the same arm forward as their forward foot. This is also how the author of a poster for a pre-war Olympics drew a runner. 

However, the problem with this is that it is the exact opposite of what people do when running. When you run the arm that is in front of the body, is the one that is the opposite of the forward foot. We have all run, a professional artist is skilled at depicting what they see. Yet, we so easily get it wrong. Why is that? 

That is because the task of running and the task of adopting a static pose of a runner are fundamentally different. They have different goals, they require a different perspective, they employ different muscles, and so on. We therefore naturally adopt a different posture to complete these two different tasks - even though when we talk about them, we think of the pose as just a snapshot of the actual run. But our mental and physical orientation is directed towards the actual task, not our expectation of what it will be.

When what we are saying we are doing and what our mind and body are actually trying to is different is a ‘task misalignment’. And how do we know that we have a task misalignment? It may take a while but a good clue is that our posture during practice is different from the posture during performance of the activity itself. 

## **Task: Key concept for understanding performance**

The idea of a task is fundamental to help us practice the right thing. Task is what you are actually doing, not what you are saying you’re doing. This is not just relevant to physical poses. Famously, we may say we are learning a subject when we are really primarily learning to pass an exam in the subject. This is important because we orient all of our efforts towards that task. So a person who is learning about something because they want to solve a problem will approach the task very differently from someone who wants to pass an exam. 

This is true even in the more extensive physical activities like distance running. We may think that the aim of a professional runner is to be able to run fast but it fact it is to win races, set records or beat opponents. This means that the practice is not only focusing on speed but on speed that peaks at particular time and can be deployed in a particular contexts. So an athlete will structure their training very carefully to be ready on race day - not just to run fast at some point. 

The problem is that our vision of what the task is, is compromised by our way of talking about it. We will say that we want to learn to play the piano but not say, we want to learn to play it so that we can play a three songs we like for pleasure. These are different tasks. 

## **Posture: How a task is revealed**

The next key concept is that of posture. Task is what our body and mind orients itself to do. It is the posture we take to solve the task. Posture here is a metaphor - it may not be an actual physical pose. But that may be a component of it.

That’s also why experts are often bad teachers of their subject - they are performing a different task. Native speakers are not always automatically good teachers of their language or translators. Teaching and translation are different tasks and when we get ready to perform them, we adopt different postures than when we are simply trying to say something.

This has both positive and negative consequences. Negative in that we often spend a lot of time practicing to adopt the wrong posture for the actual task. Positive in that the actual task does not depend so much on the sequence as described in a textbook (writing a textbook is a different task which makes the writer adopt a different posture).

So we can run before we can walk, we can learn sign language before spoken language, we can learn more difficult math before easier math, we can learn useful medical diagnostics before learning about complex chemistry. We can learn to play jazz before the classical piano or even before any basic pop-songs. All of those things are different tasks.

## **10 Task misalignment examples**

Task misalignment is incredibly common but it can also reveal much about both the mental schemas and targets for actual practice. That’s why it is important to spend a certain amount of time closely examining examples of task misalignment at different levels. 

Some common examples of when the practice of the task is misaligned with the performance. 

1. Memorising vs learning / recognition vs recall
2. Reading instead of understanding
3. Practice for performance
4. Giving examples vs doing things (what is the Czech for ‘have’ as in ‘I have done’)
5. Defining things for understanding
6. Understanding for making inferences
7. Achieving good grades for developing education
8. Being able to do something vs understanding
9. Being able to do something vs teaching (expertise vs metaexpertise)
10. Playing note sequences vs playing parts of songs

### **1 Mistaking memorisation for learning**

One of the most common problems we all experience when we are learning is remembering key concepts or patterns. In response, we make a lot of effort to memorise pairs such as word and meaning or picture and label. We often make flashcards and quiz ourselves - and now, with computers and smartphones, we even turn things into games.

In as much as having things in our head is important, this is not a bad way of building up an inventory. It is great for languages, mathematical concepts, medical conditions, geography, and many more subject. But the confusion comes at thinking that being able to recall something from a prompt as in a flashcard is the same as using it in a real context.

While we are memorising items, we are developing a skill of reacting to prompts in flashcards. That is the performance we are getting better at. And gamifying this is good for motivating us but it also leads us to optimise our performance to succeed at the game rather than develop the skill we are hoping for. Because using flashcards is in itself a task and our mind/body orient itself to solve it first and foremost. So it is possible to be very good at the ‘flashcard’ game and relatively bad at the actual task that we are memorising for. 

That’s not to underestimate the importance of memorising things - but we must think of it only as a supporting or scaffold task - not the ultimate target. In fact, rote learning has gained a very bad reputation precisely because of this. But when used in support of the task, it can be very useful.

### **2 Confusing recall and recognition**

There is a common mistake people make that is a subtype of the above error. It is confusing recognition for recall. Students often make this mistake during revision. They read something in a textbook or their notes and feel like they now remember it. But being able to recognise something is not the same as recognising it (as we have all found out during exams at some point). That’s why two-sided flashcards are so useful even if they themselves suffer from a different kind of this problem.

### **3 Reading instead of understanding**

Many students spend a lot of time reading assigned texts. But ‘reading’ is just the name of the task. It is not simply to decode the letters into sound and create mental pictures. The actual task is understanding, comparing, making connections and conclusions. Those all require different approaches and have to be practiced separately. And many of them happen before and after reading.

### **4 Mistaking practice for performance**

This is a very easy mistake we make. We are practicing something that looks like the thing we are practicing for. But it is missing a crucial element - the moment of live engagement. Whether it is actually performing in front of a live audience or simply in a context where the outcomes matter, the moment provides an important element which orients us differently. It could be simply an increased level of internal pressure or a new context. Which is why (as we’ll see below) we always have to work hard to link practice to performance and we also have to practice the elements of unpredictability in performance.

### **5 Substituting performance for practice**

The opposite confusion is also common. We are performing something every day and we are assuming that we’re also practicing. But practice is a very different task and requires different orientation and focus. We can improve through repetition of performance in this way but only with reflection and certain levels of performance will only be possible if we separate practice from regular performance.

### **6 Substituting giving examples for using them**

When somebody asks you to give an example of something you are familiar with, you often struggle. That is not because you lack knowledge or skill but because giving an example of something is a different task that requires a different orientation.

But there is is an even bigger problem. Because when we are giving an example, our entire schematic orientation changes, the examples tend to be incomplete. They follow the schema of example giving and that leads to big misconception.

Both giving examples and giving examples that actually represent what you are giving the example of is a task that requires a different kind of mental orientation and focus - which means something that can be practiced.

### **7 Substituting defining for understanding**

A special kind of task misalignment is confusing being able to define something for understanding it. This is a companion to the problem with giving examples. Giving definitions is a very different task and skill from understanding and figuring things out. 

The opposite is also true. Reading a definition is different from learning to be able to understand the definition. Something textbook authors should take to heart.

### **8 Substituting understanding for making inferences**

There’s a difference between understanding something and being able to make useful inferences about it. They are different tasks. I may be trying to understand something in order to be able to restate its definition in my own words. For example, I may try to understand the difference between voltage and wattage in electricity and be able to explain it on an exam. But it does not follow, that I can make useful inferences about the design of an electrical system. On the other hand, I may be able to do that without a full understanding of the difference. 

This is why so often curricula are misaligned with their stated goal - for example, the goal is to have a population that can deal better with their finances or make good decisions about nuanced policy issues but the curricula are designed to create a population that understands differential calculus or probability theory.

### **9 Substituting good grades for education**

Teaching or studying to the test are well-known phenomena. But understanding the task misalignment helps us better think about how they work.

Just like with gamification, the grades provide the student and her teacher a goal towards which they should both orient all their efforts. Education may be the goal, but all effort goes towards the test. It is telling that people take practice tests - not practice the skill that the test is supposed to measure. For some tests, there are entire industries that promise to prepare you for it (from books to in-person tutorials). Their advertising never mentions that you will actually be good at the thing the test measures. And indeed, you may not have to be.

### **10 Being able to do something for understanding**

This is the converse of the understanding - inferences misalignment. We assume that just being able to do something means we can explain it. But those are very different tasks. We are all native speakers of at least one language, but very few of us can name let alone describe most of the rules that govern how we speak.

### **11 Understanding for being able to explain**

Einstein supposedly said, that if you cannot explain something simply, you don’t understand it. But that is not true. Understanding and explaining are two different tasks and it is entirely possible, in fact, it is very common that we can do one and not the other. 

That is not to say that the act of explaining something does not improve our understanding. It most definitely does. But the problem is that it often improves our own understanding more than that of others. That’s why introductory texts are often not very useful to learn much about the discipline because they distil somebody’s own understanding.

Meta expertise (expertise about a subject or skill) is a separate skill because describing things is a different task from trying to understand them. They share many similarities but they are different. 

### **12 Being able to play a series of notes vs playing songs**

When people practice sight reading (playing directly from sheet music), they often spend a lot of time practicing which note they should play based on what they see in the notation. But that is a very different task from playing the song. The task of playing a song from sheet music is not to quickly react with a finger to each individual note - it is to translate patterns into a flow of music.  Therefore both require different kinds of practice. They may both contribute to the general skill of being able to play music but they are not the same.

## **Why is task misalignment so dangerous**

Other than not practicing at all, practicing the wrong thing is the most common cause for failing to improve. And we may not always know that we are practicing the wrong thing until we try a different approach.

Not being able to exactly pin-point the task should not stop us from starting to practice, but a significant part of our reflection should be about how what we are practicing actually relates to the task.

Task misalignment can have two consequences for practice:

1. Misdirection (waste of time)
2. Redirection (building scaffolding)

### **Misdirecting task misalignment**

When we completely misalign the task such as with the example of adopting a running pose, we get very little benefit for practice until we notice that misalignment. We are simply practicing the wrong thing. It is not likely that standing on one foot with the wrong arm forward is going to improve any aspect of our running. We might get some side benefits from the strength and stability training but there are most likely more useful ways of doing that.

But there are situations when practicing the ‘wrong thing’ can be useful. That’s the case of redirection of scaffolding.

### **Redirection (scaffolding)**

As we get into higher levels of performance, it is impossible to simply gain enough input by performing the task exactly. Or we need to develop some additional skill to help us practice in the first place. 

Memorising vocabulary is an example of a misaligned task that actually helps us build the scaffolding for reading comprehension or translation in the language.

A musician learning to count rhythm or to use a metronome is an example of a scaffolding that will enable that musician to actually practice rhythmic playing later on even if the thing she is practicing is not performance. 

Practicing grammatical constructions of academic language will enable us to practice composing paragraphs later on even though academic writing is not simply putting together these constructions, and so on.

sections.title: Four Approaches to Practice
sections.content:
# Four Approaches to Practice

## The importance of Practice

> “What do you do every day to improve that is similar to how a musician practices their scales?” interview question suggested by Tyler Cowen and Daniel Gross in their book Talent.
> 

Most people do not practice things to get better at them. They just do what they are doing when it comes to it and improve a little bit each time until they hit a plateau. This works for many things in life and allows us to get good enough at most things to the level we need to get by.

But there are many types of activities that simply require more focus and effort than just doing something now and again. Playing a musical instrument, speaking a foreign language, touch typing, writing  and reading are some examples of activities where focused practice is essential to even get started. But most people stop practicing even here after they get good enough and never improve beyond a certain point.

There are four approaches you can take to practice.

1. Repetitive practice
2. Reflective practice
3. Purposeful practice
4. Deliberate practice

I ordered them here by how effective they are to help you overcome the limitations of working memory to increase fluency.  But the biggest jump is in going from repetitive practice to reflective practice. In fact, reflective practice is something that you can do all the time, purposeful and deliberate practice may not always be an option.

## 1 Repetitive practice

Repetitive practice is when you just try to repeat something many times in sequence to get better at it. For example, when you repeat a word many times to try to remember it or when you study for an exam. This is better than nothing but it has severe limits. 

Apart from being boring, simply repeating things over and over does not let you combine things into bigger chunks. It also relies on having some aptitude or prior knowledge. Which is why people often give up when they try to learn something by rote and say “I’m just not very good at it.” But in fact, their attitude should be:

<aside>
💡 It’s not that I can’t learn this, I just haven’t found a way to practice it to learn it.

</aside>

But sometimes we don’t even do that much and we just rely on getting better at something by doing it multiple times. We call that experience but we should be cautious about assuming pure experience is enough to continue improving. This can be best summarised by this quote from Stephen Covey (author of the famous book ‘7 Habits of Highly Effective People’):

<aside>
💬 “experience is overrated.  Some people say they have twenty years, when in reality, they only have one year’s experience, repeated twenty times.” [How Stephen Covey Changed The Life Of One Young Entrepreneur Through A Single Powerful Phrase (forbes.com)](https://www.forbes.com/sites/kathycaprino/2015/11/02/how-stephen-covey-changed-the-life-of-one-young-entrepreneur-through-a-single-powerful-phrase/?sh=470a0cc55b2e)

</aside>

## 2 Reflective practice

Adding reflection to repetition is what makes your practice reflective. That is when you focus on the task you’re trying to practice and try to identify what chunks you could create to reduce the demands on working memory and what are the most effective ways of practicing to develop those chunks.

### **Advantage of reflective practice**

The advantage of reflective practice over purposeful or deliberate practice is that you can do it all the time. You can do much of it in your head and add in repetition when you have time. 

Reflective practice is what people who are good at what they do engage in all the time. That is how they can keep improving and exploring new areas. They are constantly thinking about what they do, how it all fits together and how to improve what they do - even just a little bit. This means that when they come to actually perform the action, they’re focused on the improvement. And that makes it easier for them to develop chunks or mental representations.

<aside>
❓ Some people seem to get by further with simple repetition than others. But this is often just an illusion because they engage in more active reflection, so that even plain repetition becomes a form of practice. For example, when the chess grandmaster Magnus Carlsen was asked about deliberate practice, he said that he finds it is not for him. But later on, when he was asked how many hours a day he thinks about chess, he responded that a better question would be how many hours he does not think about it.

</aside>

### **Disadvantage of reflective practice**

The disadvantage is that your progress is uneven and takes much longer. 

Also, this does require that you keep whatever you want to improve top of mind. If you are really interested in what you’re trying to get better at, you will always think about it. But if what you’re trying to improve at is just something you have to do, you will probably not do enough reflective repetition to truly improve.

This could be illustrated by another quote from Magnus Carlsen when asked for advice on how to get better at chess:

<aside>
💬 “I may be the worst person to ask, because for me the advice is ‘have some talent and  becomes obsessed.” [paraphrase from interview with Lex Fridman] [REF]

</aside>

Most people cannot be sufficiently obsessed about most things, so they need more structured approach to improve.

## 3 Purposeful practice

Purposeful practice is when you set an exact target for improvement and schedule time slots over a period of time to get better at it.

Even if you main mode of improvement is reflective practice, you will need to insert some bouts of purposeful practice into the process. It is especially important at the beginning of learning any new discipline or if what you are learning requires fluency (such as writing).

To develop a block of purposeful practice to improve at something, you can proceed in 5 steps:

1. Identify what aspect of your performance you want to improve (think about moments when your fluency gets disrupted)
2. Break the performance into chunks that you can practice (these are not ‘real’ chunks, just ones that you can work on)
3. Decide on how you are going to measure improvement and/or get feedback on what you do
4. Practice in blocks of effort anywhere between 10 and 90 minutes depending on the type of task (30 minute blocks are  a good default) for a total of between 6 and 20 hours depending on the level you are starting from
5. Review changes in improvement and reflect on how to fine-tune the practice work and the chunks you are trying to develop

The review is the last step on the list but you need to reflect on how things went after every practice session.

Purposeful practice is necessary to achieve a minimum level at some skills but it is also great for areas where you want to improve a little bit but that you don’t want to think about all the time. 

On the other hand, if the process of purposeful practice sounds like too much work, you can always incorporate elements of purposeful practice into your general reflective practice. But you have to get into the habit of having frequent mental check-ins with yourself and taking the time to stop the flow you’re in and repeat a certain action in a focused way.

## 4 Deliberate practice
