Deliberate practice is when you follow an established programme that is designed to increase your performance. Ideally, you do this with a coach but you always need to have a very good system of receiving feedback on your performance to help you focus your practice.

Deliberate practice in the strictest sense is not available to everyone and for any skill. These are the prerequisites:

1. Working in a discipline where it is easy to measure progress mostly along a single dimension.
2. Following a well-established programme of development that has had years of input based on the experiences of different people.
3. Working with an experienced coach who is at least at your level or one level above (unless there are good mechanisms of self-feedback)

A good examples of disciplines where deliberate practice (under different names) has been particularly successful are:

- Certain sports (particularly individual ones)
- Musical performance
- Chess
- Typing
- Memory

But elements of deliberate practice can be inserted into many other fields:

- Language learning
- Reading and writing
- Photography
- Programming
- Using computers
- Academic knowledge

The key is to find points where your performance starts to suffer because of the limitations of working memory.

Even though the Academic Writing Bootup calls itself deliberate practice, it is at heart a prescription for purposeful practice but with as much of deliberate practice inserted in as possible.

sections.title: Practice in Different Disciplines
sections.content:
# How do people practice in different disciplines

## Musical instruments

There are many lessons writers can learn from musical performance. Here are a few lessons I found particularly relevant (some of those we mentioned before):

1. Focus on the problem parts. Do not just wait for the part you have trouble with to come up, practice it in isolation. Otherwise you will never get enough opportunities to practice the things you struggle with the most.
2. Always know what you are going to practice when you sit down or pick up your instrument. Don’t just start randomly noodling. You will not get enough focused practice and will be too distracted to make the most of your time.
3. When practicing a new piece, identify the bigger repeating chunks (sometimes hundreds of notes) and think of them as one. You can watch classical pianists on YouTube describe how they do it for complex pieces and jazz musicians talking about how they use this to ‘memorise’ hundreds of jazz standards. [REF]
4. But you also need to do the opposite. When something is particularly difficult, break it down into much smaller parts to practice. These are not necessarily the most meaningful components that go together. Sometimes you practice just a two- or three- note transition between meaningful chunks.
5. Vary speed and rhythm while practicing. Slow down far below the speed you are planning to play at. Break up the rhythm first before you put it back together.
6. Transcribe what you hear while focusing on the parts. Again, you will see lots of videos on YouTube sharing transcriptions of interesting pieces of music along with analysis. Particularly, for jazz musicians transcribing solos is an essential part of the process. [REF]
7. Always practice in the context of performance. Public performance is different from practice because new possible inputs into working memory are introduced. So while you should focus on what you are practicing most of the time, sometimes you can deliberately introduce a few distractions to learn to cope with that.
8. Put limits on yourself. Only play with a few notes or just some keys, or skip certain notes.
9. Record yourself and listen back. You will be surprised how different the recording is from what you were hearing in your head while playing.
10. You can develop creativity and means of self-expression by repeating patterns and also by  initially just repeating what others do.

## Running

Running seems like it should have very few things to offer writers but in fact this whole programme was inspired by the famous Couch to 5K. Here are some of the lessons:

1. It is possible to develop stamina over relatively short period of time and to develop skills that were hard to imagine at the start. You just need to break the process down into small chunks and slowly increase them over time.
2. While this general process will work for almost anyone, there is no one precise series of steps that will accomplish that goal. There are many variations on the C25K programme and also on similar approaches that take you to longer distances and they all achieve similar results.
3. Accumulating knowledge from across many people practicing works. People have always run but the development of new training approaches have expanded running into an activity that is more accessible to more people and that has enabled more athletes at the top to continue improving beyond what was once thought possible.

Another interesting lesson from running and similar sports is that simply being alongside others increases performance - particularly if they are slightly above your own level. It is not exactly clear why or how this works but simply seeing others being able to do something seems to increase level of performance even without consciously trying to compete with them. Knowing that something is possible, makes it seem like a more achievable task.

## Chess

The biggest lesson from chess is that complex and rich chunks are absolutely essential to overcoming the limitations of working memory. Human chess players simply cannot calculate as far into the future to beat even a very simple computer. But chess masters were able to beat computers for decades by being able to draw on large patterns. Even the famous first match where Deep Blue beat Gary Kasparov, he was able to win one game and tie two. [REF]

Nowadays computers beat humans easily but it is at least in part because they started using techniques that help them recognise larger patterns in the same way human players do.

Chess is the one area where the notion of ‘deliberate practice’ is reliably known and recognised. Not all players use it in the same way but all players practice in a highly reflective way. Here are some of the things chess players do:

1. Study past games analytically and replay them on the chessboard or in their mind.
2. Analyse all of their own chess matches with input from others and focus on what they could do differently next time.
3. Focus on developing a mental inventory of large patterns such as opening moves, end games, etc.
4. Learn from others. Chess players don’t just play against other players. They talk with each other  about the games they just played or plays other people played. Often even opponents will analyse the game with each other afterward. 
5. Learn with others. Top chess champions have teams and coaches but most serious chess players are members of clubs and practice for championships.

The key lesson of chess is that you can improve with focused reflective repetition drawing on the experience of others even in a very abstract area. This is deliberate practice at its best.

The other lesson is something chess shares with music. It is that you can you can develop creativity and personal style by reflective repetition of patterns set by others. Deliberate reflective practice does not lead simply to learning to repeat, it builds an inventory of patterns that is unique to each person and that they can use in creative ways to express themselves or solve new problems they encounter.

> “You practice something and you get creative.’ Gary Kasparov [ref]
> 

The final lesson of chess is that the simple rules of how things are put together are not enough. You need to develop an ability to think in larger patterns, if you want to have any chance of productive fluency.

> One way to succeed is to have a bit of aptitude and become obsessed. Another way is to develop some interest and follow a deliberate practice plan. (Magnus Carlsen) [REF]
> 

## Memory

There are memory competitions and those competitions have champions. People will compete in disciplines such as the number of digits memorised in 5 minutes (the world record is 519 [ref]) or the sequence of playing cards.

Testing the capacity of working memory was first done with analysing how many digits people can memorise. And according to Ericsson [ref], he formulated some of the first ideas about deliberate practice when he was running experiments with number memory. This is what crystalized the idea of chunks but also the importance of learning from others.

Here are some key things we can learn from memory champions:

1. Chunking doesn’t “just” work by accident. It is the only way it can work. Recognising larger patterns and keeping them in immediate memory for later use is essential.
2. Adding meaning to chunks is essential but the meaning does not have to be intrinsic to the chunk. This is the idea behind memory palaces. You associate an item you want to quickly recall with a vivid picture in your mind that you had ‘prepared’ earlier. The title of the book “Moonwalking with Einstein” by Joshua Foer is about one such image he used to win a memory competition.
3. Visualisation is an important tool. Not everybody has the same ability to visualise vivid images in their mind but it is essential to walk through performance in your head in any way possible.
4. Anything can intrude into working memory. Memory champions often go to extremes to screen out distractions such as wearing blindfolds with pinpricks for seeing only the thing you are looking at and headsets that block out noise. Anything that can take up a valuable slot in working memory needs to be screened out. The lesson is not that we should be wearing blindfolds while practicing but that we should be paying attention to other inputs competing for a place in our working memory. At one extreme is to wear protective gear but another option is to incorporate the environmental distractions into the mental representations as part of practice.
5. Attention is important and as we saw in the example of trying to remember the long number, simply increase the level of focus makes this easier. There are limits what can be achieved with attention but it alone can reduce the load on working memory.
6. Not all skills learned through deliberate practice are easily transferable.  Just because somebody can win a memory contest, that does not mean that they will never forget their keys or somebody’s name. Their practice was all aimed at memorising digits or cards or something similar. But if they wanted to be able to do the keys, they would have to practice that. 

<aside>
📜 The journalist-turned memory champion Joshua Foer tells a story about how he went home on the bus from the New York ceremony in which he received the award for memory forgetting that he’d driven there in his car. [REF]

</aside>

## Foreign language learning by polyglots

There are many disciplines where deliberate practice has a huge potential but it is not used. Learning foreign languages is one of these. Language teaching and learning is full of practice activities. In fact, you cannot have a textbook without practice activities and often additional practice books are published.

But as a long-time language teacher (and even teacher trainer and textbook author) as well as a language learner, I can confirm that language teaching and learning falls short of the ideal of purposeful practice in multiple ways. It is both in methods and assumptions. In short, traditional language teaching largely focuses on two things:

1. long-term rather than working memory 
2. practice with respect to the requirements of the textbook, rather than the task

I tried to outline a how some of the lessons of deliberate practice could be inserted into language learning in Building your language muscle [REF].

However, there is one area in language learning where we can learn some serious lessons and that is the people who have learned multiple languages called polyglots. Learning another language feels almost like a magical task that requires special aptitude to most people. This may make it seem like there’s nothing to learn from polyglots who surely must have preternaturally developed abilities. But that is not the case. What sets polyglots apart from casual language learners is:

1. Enough interest in the task that it motivates them to spend time and effort
2. Techniques that draw on the ideas of deliberate practice (even if this is not done explicitly)

Both are important lessons for improving academic writing. Academic writing, is after all like a foreign language to many native speakers and a literal foreign language to many more writers. It also requires some investment in time and effort but the good news is that it much less than acquiring and maintaining fluency in 3 or more languages.

There are many accounts of how polyglots learn languages but we can draw on two. First, about what polyglots have in common. A [video on what polyglots do differently](https://youtu.be/ROh_-RG3OVg) by the Slovak polyglot Lýdia Machová lists 10 features of practice common to the people who can master multiple languages. Here we will focus on these:

1. Polyglots do not all have the same method. What they have in common is dedication of time and effort.
2. Polyglots do not learn the majority of their skill in the classroom. In fact, most of them learn in on their own, drawing in others as necessary for resources.
3. Polyglots mostly do not use textbooks. They draw on their own materials to fit their needs. They spend a lot of time preparing practice materials.
4. Polyglots have developed techniques that allow them to get as much practice as possible with useful feedback for further learning. They achieve this by:
    1. using the languages in practice as much as possible (both speaking and listening)
    2. not being afraid of mistakes but accepting them as part of the learning process
    3. doing as much as possible with what they have (simplifying where possible)
5. Polyglots develop positive attitudes to the acts of practice. 
6. Polyglots practice in small chunks. They find it more effective to study 60 minutes a day than 5 hours in one day.

Polyglots also set their own targets based on performance and carefully monitor progress.

The other lesson we can draw from Fluent in Three Months by Benny Lewis [REF]:

> In the initial stages, try to build a large inventory of usable chunks focused on performance. But as you want to progress to more advanced levels of performance, you need to start drawing on knowledge of principles of how language is put together.  [REF] - paraphrase
> 

The language teaching community has also spent a lot of time thinking about competence and how to assess it. This has resulted in two similar frameworks for judging how “good” someone is based on what they are able to achieve in the real world. We will use these as an inspiration for defining competence in academic writing.

sections.title: Timing of Practice
sections.content:
# Timing of practice: How long and how often does it take

## Timing is crucial

Starting from very limited skill level is a very emotionally taxing experience. The task ahead of us seems insurmountable and every step we take seems to take us no closer to our goal. This leads many people to give up before they even get started. But if we know how long to expect, we can be sure even the smallest step is a real progress in the right direction. These steps accumulate and when we look back it seems impossible we were ever able to travel the distance.

There are two broad questions we want to know:

1. How long will it be until our performance improves so that we can be fluent enough to do meaningful work?
2. How often and how long should my practice sessions be?

Each of these larger questions contain additional puzzles such as:

1. Can we break the larger goal into subgoals?
2. What happens when we take a break from practice?
3. Does it matter what time of day we practice?
4. and so on….

The bad news is that we don’t know the precise answer to any of these questions. But the good news is that we have a very good idea about the rough parameters based on the shared experiences of many different types of people over many disciplines. And it seems that as long as you stick within them, you can be confident of success. 

The other good news is that there is a lot of scope for you to modify a programme that fits your situation as long as you stick to the basic principles..

## Total amount of time: 10,000 vs 20 hours

How long does it take to develop fluent expertise? The scary number that was made popular by Malcolm Gladwell is 10,000 hours over about 10 years [REF]. That is a more or less correct number for people at the top of their field. 

But can you develop enough fluency to be able to perform adequately at a skill where you start with nothing in less time? Or can you overcome a plateau of performance in less time?

The answer to those questions is yes. And the number made popular by Josh Kaufman [REF] is 20 hours. That is about the amount of time of real practice in which you can:

1. Learn to run 5 kilometers from nothing
2. Learn to play a few songs on a musical instrument
3. Learn to touch type
4. Learn to speak enough of a foreign language to talk about yourself or order food in a restaurant
5. Learn to read confidently in another alphabet (Russian or Greek)

Now, this is not 20 hours in classes, or 20 hours of reading. It is 20 hours of concerted practice. But it means that is you practice for 30 minutes 5 times a week, you can achieve meaningful progress in 4 - 8 weeks.

Which is why many programmes we mentioned are spread over about 8 weeks. You can probably compress this into as little as 4 weeks and expand it to 12 weeks but this is a good benchmark.

Also, there’s nothing precise about 20 hours. Couch to 5K probably adds up to about 16 hours of running, an introductory language learning session may be closer to 30 hours. 

If you are not starting from absolute scratch and you just want make progress with a component of a larger skill, you could probably even make meaningful progress over 3-6 hours over about 2 weeks. This is how long it may take a musician to truly master a new song, for example.

So, here are some **recommendations** for how to allocate time to developing or improving performance improvement:

1. For your larger goals, allocate anywhere between 15 and 30 hours over 8 to 12 weeks; this will be about 1.5 and 4 hours a week over 3 to 5 days.
2. You could probably compress this into a 4 week period by practicing about an hour a day. Some skills are more amenable to this than others but there are limits. Practicing 30 hours for a week will not let you develop your skills as 30 hours over 2-3 months. 
3. Do not try to set goals for much further into the future than 12 weeks. In fact, you may benefit from splitting your 8-12 week programmes into shorter sprints to give you enough of a chance to evaluate your progress.
4. For your smaller learning goals, allocate into anywhere between 3 and 6 hours over 2-3 weeks; this will be about 1.5 to 3 hours a week
5. You should probably schedule some rest days and give yourself time to consolidate. 
6. Some of the time should be spent reflecting and recalibrating goals. Whether that time counts as practice will depend on the type of activity. Thinking about running goals and form will help you improve very little, thinking about music, chess or writing in a targeted way may actually contribute to improved performance. But it should probably not be much more than about 10% of your overall time spent on the activities.

**Note**: The times above are based on what is a sensible time commitment for most people who are serious about improvement. They are consistent with what people report but we do not have systematic evidence that would let us be more specific. 

The times will vary based on your current level of skill. Complete novices may see quick improvement over shorter periods of practice time but will not be able to benefit from cramming more time into a shorter span.

People closer to the peak performance may only see very little improvement after a lot of effort. But they will often be able to achieve that improvement by adding more practice time to every day. 

For example, a beginner musician may be able to play a few songs at a satisfactory level after 20 hours of practice spread over a month in a way that they would not be able to if they crammed 30 hours into the first week. But a professional musician may require 20 hours just to perfect one section of a larger song to a public performance standard. But they may be able to achieve that improvement by practicing 3 hours a day for a week.

## Practice session length

The next question we should answer is how long should individual practice sessions be. The recommended number varies but 30 minutes is a good starting point. It is sufficiently short for most people to be able to focus and sufficiently long that a meaningful amount of work can be done. 

However, even practice sessions as short as 10 minutes can make a significant contribution to improvement. Particularly if the skill being practiced is more of a building block. Memorising vocabulary or practicing forms or scales are all things that can be done in 10-minute increments over the course of a day.

But even some aspects of writing can be done in 10 minute increments. In fact, being able to do something in just 10 minutes, may in itself be a skill to develop [REF - Ninja writing].

In the initial stages, you will definitely benefit more from two 30 minute practice sessions over two days than one 60 minute session and then skipping a day. People often talk about the consolidation that happens during sleep. That is plausible but we do not know for certain.

However, there are other types of activities that require sustained focus for longer than 30 minutes or at least several 30-minute blocks with short breaks between. This is important particularly for activities where so called ‘flow’ is a desired state. This will be particularly important for writing where scheduling 90 min writing sessions will be an important part of the process. 

But remember, we need to distinguish between doing ‘work’ for 90 minutes and practicing with purpose for 90 minutes. Simply repeating a task does not lead to an improvement after a while. In fact, it seems that after people reach a plateau, they regress slightly if they just continue to repeat what they learned. 

Plateau is a negative word but we can also think about it as reaching the level you need to perform at high enough quality and with sufficient fluency to reach your goal. This is fine. But often external circumstances change something about the environment or your aims and desires change and the current level won’t be enough.

This is where many people feel like they reached the end of their potential but with focused reflective practice, they can almost always break through the plateau and improve (even if only a little bit). 

If you find yourself in this situation, you will often benefit from working in shorter sessions but with more focus on improving performance. 

## Practice times and routines

What is the best time of day to practice? As with all of these questions, there is a relatively simple answer but with much variation. 

The simple answer is, practice whenever you can get the most out of the allocated time. That’s when you can focus the most. For many people that is early in the morning but for some late at night. 

Right after lunch or an intensive meeting, your energy is probably depleted so that you won’t get the most out of your practice session. Particularly for writing, it is best to do your practice session before you did your reading - or in other words, read the day before, make notes, but when you start practicing your writing, start before you had a chance to set your thoughts in many different directions.

<aside>
📜 Out first, in second. -- CGP Grey on writing scripts for educational videos

</aside>

Of course, one of the things you are practicing could be overcoming tiredness and distraction. Athletes talk about learning to ‘run on tired legs’. You can use the same attitude for developing skills to work during times of day that is not the best for you. Develop switching muscles.

You should have a reliable practice routine at the time that suits you best but you should not be so dependent on that routine that even the smallest disruption to it will stop you from practicing. Because when it comes down to it any practice time is better than none.

sections.title: Identifying Need for Practice
sections.content:
# Reflection as a method for identifying need for practice

## Why is reflection important

The key component to success in practice is reflection. We know that from a lot of research on metacognition. 

As an example, we can explore a common myth that young children are good at learning languages. Young children (under the age of about 10) are good at acquiring a language in the same way we all have done it. They can even do it for multiple languages at a time. But children are horrible at learning a foreign language in school if by learning we mean going to class for two hours a week and maybe doing some homework in between. That is because their ability to develop concepts and rely on them to guide their practice is not yet as sophisticated. 

A committed adult can learn as much in a week of intense study as a child in a year of attending classes in this way. That is because they have experience they can draw on and ability to regulate their learning. Teaching a child a few grammar rules will just confuse them. Teaching an adult a few grammar rules will accelerate their learning. Of course, the rules should be simple and only there to guide practice but they make a lot of difference. 

But an even more important reason for reflection about where we are is that without it, we end up practicing the wrong thing. Here we can learn some lessons from musicians. When learning or practicing a song, don’t always start playing it from the beginning. Practice the bits you find difficult. Otherwise you end up being really good at the start of the song and never will figure out the difficult bits later on. 

## What to reflect on or signals that you need to practice

### **Speed**

The first signal that something is wrong with your performance is that you slow down. There is no absolute perfect speed for writing or anything (unless you are literally racing) but there is a minimal speed for you to be able to do it at all. 

Being able to write 700 words in 30 minutes does not make you a better writer. But not being able to write at least 200 when you do know what you want to write will make you a struggling writer. You will spend so much time fiddling about with each individual word or sentence that you will constantly keep running into limits of working memory and find it difficult to think about what you’re writing. 

### **Fluency**

Fluency is different from speed. You can write very fast but if you do it in stops and starts, you will suffer from the same effects on working memory. That does not mean that you cannot pause in the middle of a sentence to think about what you’re going to say next but you should not find yourself stopping in the middle of a phrase or a word (too often). 

The same goes for other kinds of performance. When you try to run fast, at some point your form will start to suffer and you will have to go back to focus on it. The same goes for playing a musical instrument. You can speed up a lot but your expression will suffer.

So, the lesson is that sometimes you have to slow down to increase your fluency. And only after your fluency is up, you can start speeding up again.

### **Accuracy**

When speaking, reading or writing, the name of the game is ‘fluency and accuracy’. That is the heart of the definition of dyslexia “condition that interferes with fluent and accurate reading and writing”. But dyslexia is not the only thing that does this. Speaking or writing in a foreign language (including academic language) does the same thing. 

So the other signal that you should start reflecting on your performance is when you start making more errors than usual. 

However, at the most basic level, fluency is more important than accuracy. Particularly for writing. You can always go and fix your errors. And what’s even more important is that focus on accuracy can interfere with fluency. If you are constantly thinking about being accurate, your working memory will be swamped and you won’t be able to keep up the fluency needed.

That’s why copy editors can read through a whole book and not know much about what it was about, because all they were focusing on was grammar and spelling.

### **Emotion**

<aside>
💬 Don’t think about how bad you feel during practice when nothing seems to going right, think about how great you feel in a week or two when this is easy. (inspired by Victor Wooten)

</aside>

Another signal that you should start reflecting on how you could practice to improve your performance is stress. And feelings of stress are a good signal that your working memory is being swamped and you can’t do the thing you’re trying to do.

People who move to a new country and have to speak a different language the whole day are often exhausted by the end of the day. Their working memory is constantly under siege and as a result everything takes more time and more effort.

The emotion that accompanies dyslexia is often the biggest issue. When you finish a bit of reading or writing and feel so exhausted and dispirited that you want to cry, you develop a feeling of hate towards the activity. And dyslexic children who develop greater fluency that this isn’t the case for them any more completely change their feelings, as well.

So feeling bad during doing something should not be a signal to you that the activity is not right for you or that it is just inherently awful. When you feel bad while doing something, it should be a signal that you should focus on the thing that weighs you down and practice it until the weight is lifted.

The mantra should not be: “Practice makes perfect” but “Practice makes happy.”

sections.title: Techniques for Deciding What to Practice
sections.content:
# Techniques for deciding what to practice

### Six methods for deciding what to practice

Deciding on which mental representations will actually be useful to help us with performance is the most difficult part. Which is why it is best if we can follow an established programme (such as the Couch to 5K for running). But this is not always possible. In those cases, we have to find our own path. This takes more time but it has some benefit because it helps us reflect on the process and journey.

Here is what you need:

1. Establish a feedback loop
2. Reflect on break points
3. Establish measurement
4. Retrace your steps
5. Build scaffolding
6. Learn from others

### 1 Establish a feedback loop

This is the most important component of any practice. You need feedback to help you judge your performance but most importantly changes to performance. This is easy for things like running where all you need is the objective measurements of distance and time. These can be supplemented by measures of exertion such as heart rate. But even here, subjective or semi subjective measures come into play. Perception of effort or running form form an important part of the development of a runner.

But effective feedback loops exist even in much more subjective disciplines such as musical performance. They do have an objective component (number of errors, keeping to rhythm, etc.) but even subjective components such as expressiveness can be evaluated.

Every discipline has some objective and some subjective sources of feedback, as well as some in between. For example, in here are some in academic writing:

- Objective
    - Spelling or grammar errors
    - Choice of vocabulary
    - Number of words written
    - Length of sentences
    - Correctness of citations
- Semi-subjective
    - Accuracy of paraphrasing a position
    - Correctness of assertions
    - Cohesion or coherence
    - Conformance to genre conventions
    - Readability
- Subjective
    - Persuasiveness of argument
    - Stylistic beauty
    - Feelings about the writing process
    - Feelings about how accurately you expressed what you wanted to say

There may be other measures that are relevant to you. You can find them by:

- Analysing feedback from others (explicit or implicit)
- Comparing your output to that of others (quality or quantity)
- Reflecting on your emotions

### 2 Reflect on breakpoints

Once you have an effective feedback loop, you can get information about where you need to improve. You have to do two things:

1. Reflect on what the source of the issue is.
2. Reflect on how you could break down the activity into smaller chunks to practice and develop more effective mental representations.

For example, you feel that you don’t write enough during your writing sessions. You’ve measured it and you only write 100 words in 30 minutes even when you do know what you want to write and would like to increase it to 200 words. 

1. Think about when you stopped or slowed down. Was it because
    1. You did not know how to start
    2. You did not know how to express what you want to say
    3. You stopped and rephrased every part of a sentence or you agonised over every word
    4. You had to look up too many words in the dictionary
2. Which ever of these issues is slowing you down, you can then think about breaking it down into smaller components to practice
    1. If starting a sentence or writing is a problem, only focus on that. Think further about at which point you feel most pressure and think about how you could focus on just the point.
    2. What parts of expressing yourself were the problem? Words, academic phrasing, paragraph composition? Any one of these could be practiced.
    3. If you stop frequently, analyse why. Which aspects could you practice to get better at?
    4. What kinds of words do you most often look up? What is the problem? 

### 3 Establish measurement

Measuring your performance and changes over time is essential to successful practice. It gives you focus about what to practice, suggests new directions, and also helps with monitoring about whether you are practicing the wrong thing. But seeing your progress can also motivate you to do more. 

In short, we can say that measurement plays two different roles in practice:

1. Direction
2. Motivation

How and what you measure is a more difficult question. We already gave examples of what to measure in the section on establishing a feedback loop. Now let’s have a look at how to do it. Essentially, there are two categories:

1. External measures such as speed, quantity, error rate
2. Perception of effort such as feelings of tiredness, how hard an activity is, or how we feel about the quality of our performance or even the activity itself

To improve, you should always keep an eye on where you are at the moment and reflect on whether you are getting better or worse. But for specific improvements you need to keep records. 

For example, in writing it is easy to keep track of both subjective and objective measures of your writing:

1. Keep a log of writing times and words written
2. Keep a diary of your feelings about writing
3. Count the number of spelling or grammar errors your spelling checker found

You can then compare changes over time and think about what you did to make that change.

But how do you measure the quality of your writing? How do you know whether you are writing in the way that will fit in with people in your discipline? Here you can use several comparative techniques.

1. Reading for writing
2. Flash paraphrasing

When you **read for writing**, return to some important papers in your discipline you had read and focus on the various phrases and expressions that make it seem special. Make a list of them and see how many of them can you use in your own writing. You can also go to a writing guide such as the ‘Academic Phrasebank’ and see how many of the phrases the authors you are reading are using.

Do not just go from the phrasebank to your own writing. Find the examples in your discipline first. Then try to internalise them (you can even make flashcards with sentences in which they were used) and then measure how many you naturally start using.

You will eventually find that this comes to you quite naturally. That is how people who ‘are good at writing’ learned it (they just did it informally).

Another more targeted approach is what we might call **flash paraphrasing**. This was inspired by this quote:

> “[Benjamin Franklin] first set out to see how closely he could reproduce the sentences in an article once he had forgotten their exact wording. So he chose several of the articles whose writing he admired and wrote down short descriptions of the content of each sentence—just enough to remind him what the sentence was about. After several days he tried to reproduce the articles from the hints he had written down.” (from Peak by Anders Ericsson)
> 

A similar recommendation was made by Stanley Fish in his book on ‘How to write a sentence’. The ideas is that you start by replicating sentences and focusing on the parts that make them tick.

### 4 Retracing your steps

When you are finding your own path to improvement or even when you work with a coach, you sometimes find yourself going down blind alleys and have to retrace your steps. For example, it turns out that what you are practicing is not a meaningful part of the performance, or you are working with chunks that are too small or too large.

This is a part of the process and you should embrace it. It will not feel great at the time but you should always appreciate the learning opportunity. 

With exercise, they say, if it does not hurt, you’re not doing it right. With learning it is the same. But you should always be on the look out for the right kind of pain and wrong kind of pain. The right kind of pain is tiredness and soreness. This leads to growth and you can even appreciate the pain as leading to the satisfaction of your goals. The wrong kind of pain is one that leads to injury. It is not always easy to tell which kind of pain you are experiencing. 

Which is where reflection plays such a vital role. Take note of your discomfort and how you felt later. You can then use that lesson to remind yourself next time you experience that the pain passed, that you’d been there before and it led to a good result. 

### 5 Building scaffolding

Not all things you practice are a part of the target performance. But they are still necessary to develop the skill. 

For example, when you speak a language, you don’t really use individual words very often. You speak in sentences. But as part of the learning process, it is very helpful to memorise lots of vocabulary using flashcards. You can then use that in developing your ability to speak in conversation even though, flashcards would not help you have a proper dialogue. Children do not use flashcards to learn their first language but very few adults can learn a new language well without some component of rote memorisation. 

But not all of this scaffolding is easy. It may in itself be a skill that you can get better at with practice. There are useful and less useful ways of using flashcards to memorise vocabulary. There are good and bad strategies for converting that memorisation into an ability to have a fluent conversation.

So, you may have to spend some time working on the process of memorisation. Read some guides, dry different digital tools, make or find flashcards, etc. This may seem like it’s not a real part of the process, something that doesn’t count. But it takes time and effort and without it the rest of your practice would not be as effective.

There are many types of scaffolding involved in academic writing. It could be simply typing, keyboard shortcuts that make writing in your word processor faster, learning how to use a reference manager. But it could even be things like spelling, learning academic vocabulary, getting better at grammar, etc. And it definitely involves behaviours and habits that enable your to write. 

Every single item on the above list is a skill that you can improve with practice. It may not have to be your main focus for very long but do not neglect it. Without it, the rest of the practice will be less effective. 

### 6 Learn from others

<aside>
💬 “Follow no one, listen to everyone.” Dean Karnazes, American Ultramarathon runner

</aside>

Deliberate practice at its most effective is when you can build on the experiences of others who came before you. That’s why most elite performers work with coaches and spend time reflecting on  the process.

You should build learning from others into your reflection. Read books or articles about writing. Watch YouTube videos of people talking about their writing. Have conversations with others about it.

But most importantly, you need to feed those lessons into what and how you practice. Try them out and see how they work for you.

Do not discount ideas from any corner but also do not think that there is only one way that can work for everyone. In fact, nothing works for everyone.

But do not judge whether something works for you until you’ve tried and measured the outcomes. And also do not think that what does not work for you now, will never work for you. Keep a list of things that sound intriguing to you and try them.

<aside>
💡 Everything works for someone, nothing works for everyone.

</aside>

Finally, learn about practice techniques from other disciplines. Not everything will be directly applicable but many of the strategies, approaches to planning, and attitudes, will be useful. In the next section we will have a look at some lessons we can learn from other disciplines.

sections.title: Methods for Improving Repetition
sections.content:
# What good practice looks like: 7 Methods for Improving Repetition

Now, lets have a look at the sort of activities you can use to practice almost anything. 

Remember, our target is to overcome the limits of our working memory. There three ways to do that:

1. **Focus:** decrease distractions
2. **Offload:** use some external medium like a piece of paper
3. **Practice:** increase the size of the chunks

Only practice leads to sustained improvement. It does that by developing embodied mental schemas that can be inserted into it as chunks. We have talked about how to identify those mental schemas (or representations) to target, lets now talk about how to develop them.

As always, we are relying on the experience of others rather than a deep scientific insight into what our brains look like on the inside. But, for the most part, we don’t see any great contradictions between the two.

## Characteristics of a “true” practice session

How do you know that you have had a true deliberate practice session? For a session to count as practice, it should:

1. **Have a practice target:** Before you start your session, know what you are going to practice. It is so easy to waste your time by thinking about what to do. 
2. **Focus the practice session on one thing**: Do not try to practice too many things at once. Ideally, you are just focusing on one aspect of your performance. Sometimes, you may combine more than one but then treat them as one.
3. **Focus on problems only:** Repeating on what you already know well is not helping. You should try to push yourself and that requires that you repeat the areas where you struggle.
4. **Log what you’re doing:** Make a record of what you did. Combine qualitative and quantitative aspects - how much you wrote, how you felt about the process or how you feel about the outcome. This will become very important later on but even during the time, it will help you solidify the outcomes of the session. Do NOT think of the practice session as finished until you have made a note about it (it is better to shorten the practice time and take some notes and reflect than not to reflect at all).
5. **Plan for next time:** This takes us back to point 1. If you make a plan for what you should be doing during the next practice session, it will make it easier to come to the next one prepared for success. This can very much be a part of your reflection and logging process but it is better to make it explicit because not having clear tasks at the start of practice is probably the most common cause for people not making the most of their time or even skipping the practice / work session altogether.

This brings up an important question! What if my practice session is not a ‘true’ deliberate practice session? Remember, any practice is better than no practice.

Maybe you haven’t remembered to set a practice target last time - or you find that it was the wrong target. Still, you will at least get some practice.

Or maybe you haven’t logged what you did. But hopefully, you made a mental note of what you did and that gave you some space for reflection.

<aside>
💡 Any practice is better than no practice.

</aside>

### Does work count as practice?

Next question is: Can you combine work and practice? Does doing the actual tasks you are practicing count as practice? The answer is, possibly but only if you are getting enough feedback. 

As we saw, people often regress slightly after they have reached a plateau. That is because normal repetition of the task does not give enough feedback for improvement. Also, in normal practice some of the tasks that you are most likely to need practice to improve do not come up often enough to give you actual repetition.

Andy Matuschak [REF] describes his experience of getting worse at sight reading sheet music because he did it less as part of his learning of more advanced pieces. At the same time, his lack of skill at sight reading made it more difficult for him to progress further. 

Research shows [REF] that doctors get much better at diagnosing their patients with experience up to a certain point and then they regress slightly because they stop paying attention to improving and many of the issues they may need to diagnose simply do not come up often enough for them to keep up their skills.

So, simply doing something regularly (even if it feels like every day) will not help you improve. But you can certainly insert some elements of true practice into your work. Most important of these is reflection and focused repetition. If you reflect on what you are doing, you will notice choke points. You can then introduce little bouts of focused repetition to help you improve.

Reflection without action is not enough and neither is action without reflection. But the reflection must not be confused with meditation. The reflection has to be deliberative. It has to focus on performance and building the sort of embodied mental schemas that can be used to overcome limitations of working memory. 

What this means in practice is that if you want to improve while doing the actual work, you have to inject elements of deliberate practice. This will mean that you will sometimes have to pause and repeat something you did (maybe several times and in different ways) and assess how it contributes to your performance. 

Which brings us to the question of what actual practice will look like.

### What does practice look like? What kinds of activities should you perform?

So far, we’ve been talking about why practice, what to practice towards, and how to structure programme of practice. This is not an accident. In many ways knowing the goal of practice, how to apply it, and so on, is more important. The actual practice activities will offer themselves naturally and will differ based on what you came to practice. But using some clear examples and lessons from others,  will help you save time and avoid too many dead ends. (While remembering that some dead ends are inevitable and are a part of the learning process).

## 7 Methods for Improving Practice

At heart, practice is nothing more than pure repetition of patterns of performance in a feedback rich environment. We already discussed the importance of feedback and broad patterns of performance. But here are some typical and effective approaches to making the repetition more effective.

1. Varying the size of chunks
2. Substitution
3. Back chaining
4. Varying speed
5. Adding rhythm
6. Adding constraints
7. Adding visualisation

### **Varying the size of chunks**

Chunking is the ultimate target but also a very powerful method. When repeating, vary the size of chunks you work with. When you repeat, try with the smallest possible chunks first, then increase them in size. And then reduce them again but using different boundaries. This technique is very common in language learning but also in music, and runners use it, as well.

Here is an example of how you could use the technique to practice the Czech example above:

> You want to internalise the pattern for *Staré knihy jsou támhle* (old books are over there) so that you can perform some actions with it*.* Start with *staré knihy* (old books) and then *jsou támhle* (are over there) but also add *knihy jsou* (books are) into the mix. And then combine these chunks in different ways *staré knihy jsou* (old books are) and *knihy jsou támhle* (books are over there).
> 

### **Backchaining**

Backchaining is the same as varying the size of chunks but starting from the end. You can do it for individual components of larger patterns. In language, it works at the level of words, sentences or even paragraphs. But in other disciplines it may only work for certain components or actions. 

> So in the example above, you would start repeating ‘*hle’* then add ‘*tám*’ to it to make up ‘*támhle*’. Or should start with *jsou* and then add *knihy* to the front of it to make up *knihy jsou*. The principle is obvious but people often do not realise how many variations there are.
> 

### **Varying speed**

In real life, performance happens in many speeds. Speed is usually not the primary target of practice (unless you are practicing for a race or typing championship) but fluency is. Being in control over speed is very important. In some ways, that is the definition of fluency.

So, it is not the speed that is important but the variation. Speed up and slow down. Repeat in different bursts of speed. Have sessions that focus on repeating things very slowly, sessions where you focus on speed, and sessions where you vary.

Of the different speed variations, slowing down is probably the most effective. This is probably because most people find it unnatural. What you should is repeat something so while slowing down to the point of feeling strange and then try to stay at that speed. Use this slow speed to really focus on your performance. 

When speeding up, don’t just rush to get it over with. Speed up with a purpose. Even if just for a short burst to get used to the idea of greater speed. Set a timer or even a metronome (see below) and slowly increase it with each repetition.

To continue with our example above:

> Have flashcards of a number of words and flip them around for increasingly short periods of time to see how well you can recognise the words. 

Next start speaking the words and phrases as slowly as possible. First, do it in English to get used to the idea. Then in Czech. Slow down more and more. 

Next vary the speed, pronounce one word very slowly and then the next one as fast as possible.

Start recording yourself. Record yourself while speaking very slow and then much faster. Is your pronunciation still as accurate at the higher speed? Again, speed without accuracy is no good.
> 

One of the reasons varying speed is so useful is that it involves the whole body. Even if you are trying to speed up just in your mind, your posture changes (either literal or metaphorical). You become more involved, increase focus. And also reduce boredom.

### **Add rhythm**

As we started playing around with speed, we started to introduce elements of rhythm almost without trying. It is important to do this explicitly, to take advantage of the bodily nature of speed work.

There are many ways you can do this depending on the activity:

1. Start tapping a rhythm with your foot or hand
2. Create a chant that follow a certain rhythm (it could be a march or a flowing rhythm as in classical music or a choir)
3. Listen to different music in the background varying speed and beat (usually you want to keep it to instrumental music but in very physical activities music with words may be fine)
4. Use a metronome and set it to different speeds (there are many apps that will do this for you)

This is very easy to do with language. In fact, there are books published that do this for English (Jazz chants):

> To practice *knihy jsou*, you can:
1. sing it to a different songs
2. clap your hands at the start of each word
3. clap your hands at start of each syllable
> 

Of course, you can and should combine speed and rhythm with all the other variations we’ve seen so far.

### **Substitution**

Substitution is essential. You cannot just repeat the same thing over and over. So, substitute the parts of the pattern you are repeating. Again, this is at the heart of language learning (and writing) but is common to most practice. To continue with the example above:

> The next step would be to learn to substitute other words into the same pattern *new*, *cheap*, *good* for *old*, or *here* for *over there.* And so on. You would then repeat them in different combinations until they the whole pattern becomes one flexible chunk you can read without processing individual components.
> 

Substitution is essential when you want to progress and you want to build more generalised schemas. Repeating the same thing over and over without adding other contexts will not be enough to develop more general schemas.

For example, when learning a language, all the repetition we have done so far would work for a single sentence or maybe a handful of phrases that would serve you well on a holiday abroad. But not for a whole language. 

### **Adding constraints and changing contexts**

> You have to train for making mistakes. James Hoffman, world barista champion [REF]
> 

You almost never get to do what you do in ideal conditions. But it is not just matter of conditions, it is the variation in what you do. Your embodied mental schemas have to be flexible enough to adapt to new inputs or drive your change. 

One very useful way to expand the flexibility of your mental schemas is to introduce constraints into your practice. These could be natural or artificial.

**Natural constraints** are the sort of things that may happen to you when you need to perform an action. For example, there may be noise, or you may be interrupted by pop ups on your computer. Or you may have limited time, or feel really exhausted.

You can focus on these in your practice. Practice in noisy conditions, have your email client or Twitter open next to your word processor and practice not looking at it. Or commit to writing 3 times for 10 minutes in a day rather than once for 30 minutes and do it after a meeting or after a meal.

This has to be deliberate. Do NOT use this as an excuse to have bad practice hygiene. Make sure that you identify a condition you are trying to practice and focus on designing practice conditions you want to improve it. You must also take note of your response to the disruption and improvement under those conditions.

Remember, it is not a good idea to introduce a lot of distraction into your practice routine without a purpose.

**Artificial constraints** are paradoxically more useful than natural constraints. They serve two purposes:

1. Provide more avenues of developing flexible and usable embodied schemas
2. Make practice more varied and enjoyable

There is a whole approach to coaching in some sports that is built around artificial constraints. For example, a catcher in a game may be thrown foam balls or players learning to catch balls have to catch irregular objects instead. Of course, they still practice with regular balls most of the time but these constraints serve to develop more flexibility.

Musicians will often practice with just one hand or by skipping certain keys on their instrument. A common practice for developing musical sensibility is to play expressively with just one or two notes. 

In language related practice, like writing, there are many opportunities for introducing artificial constraints that will clearly help you develop different schemas better. Here are some examples:

- Avoid words beginning with letters H and W
- Don’t use the letter J at all
- Never start your sentence with a noun
- Write a paragraph where every last word in a sentence is a rhyme on the previous one
- Limit your sentences to 12 words
- Write every sentence with 32 words or more
- Write every other sentence from back to front

Unlike with the natural constraints which should be used sparingly and more deliberately, you can introduce artificial constraints more often just to spice up your practice routine. Because they are so artificial, they will not lead you to develop bad habits but will rather make you a more flexible performer.

### **Location and time changes**

One specialised way of adding constraints is to change locations and times of practice. Having stability is important to habit formation which help you ensure you practice regularly. For example, having a stable place to write or practice your vocabulary can be very useful. You may find it easier to get started and focus better when you are in your comfortable place. The same goes for having a regular schedule.

And you should spend significant time and effort to establish such times and places when you do your best work. Particularly, when you are starting out. But performance does not always happen in one time or place. And even if it did, you may not always be able to pick your time or place.

That’s why it is important to practice varying the time and place you do your practice. Again, this should not be something that may or may not happen. Be deliberate about it. If you find, that you can only do practice or work at a certain time and place, practice doing it at different times. For instance, write at the end of the day instead of at the beginning once a week. Or do your drills in the park or cafe, instead of a at home.

### **Adding meaning through visualisation**

As I keep repeating, pure repetition is not enough. We don’t get better any more after a while by mindlessly repeating the same thing. All the techniques we discussed so far will automatically inject a bit of reflection into your repetition. This will help you develop better, more flexible representations (embodied mental schemas) that will then become available to working memory as usable chunks when you need them.

It seems that these chunks can be very large and one thing that makes them richer and more usable is meaning. It is easy to loose sight of the meaning as you are repeating what you are doing - even when you vary the repetition. But you should always keep your practice meaningful.

Visualisation is a powerful way to inject meaning into your practice. As you are practicing, thing about using the skill in a real context. Imagine your conversation partner, imagine your readers, or imagine the place you will run through. If you watch professional skiers before a race, you will see that alongside stretching and warming, they have their eyes closed and move their body in different shapes. They are running the course in their mind - they are using visualisation. 

Do that as often as possible. 

Not everyone can easily recall rich images in their mind at will. But you can always rehearse the context verbally in your head. Just think about all the steps you have to take. There are two ways to add meaning through visualisation:

1. **Internal to the activity:** Visualise the time and place where you do something. Think about the people around you, think about the purpose, think about what it will look like during or after. This could as simple as saying: ‘when I sit at my computer, I will click here to open Word, and then click in the last paragraph and start writing’ or it could be more elaborate. But when you practice, always think about what it will look and feel like when you do it in the real context. For example, when you are practicing vocabulary with a flashcard, think about using the word or phrase in context. But that does not just mean “in a sentence”. Visualise yourself saying or writing this in a real situation or several. Visualisation is like free travel.
2. **External to the activity:** Not all of your visualisation has to be about what you are practicing. Sometimes you can use mnemonic devices to build useful associations. That is how the famous ‘mental palace technique’ works. You associate the thing you want to remember with a powerful image, so that it is easier to recall, focus and remove other distractions. But that is also how motivational mantras work. As you are practicing, think to yourself about how much you are going to enjoy being better at what you are doing. Then when you are doing it, you can think back and appreciate all the work you’ve done. It’s a virtuous cycle.

### **Practicing to practice**

All of the techniques for improving practice are skills. And skills need practice to get better at them. This is how scaffolding works. If you want to build a building, you have to build a scaffold to help you. Without it, you can’t build the building. But it is work, it takes time and resources. 

So, you should spend some time to practice your practice techniques. Reflect on whether you are doing them right and what you could improve. You don’t have to spend a lot of time on most of them but allocate about 5% of your practice time to this.

Sometimes, the technique itself is so complicated that it is its own skill. Or at least for some people. For example, many beginning musicians struggle to use the metronome or to count to help them keep rhythm. That in itself is a skill to develop and requires its own practice even if it is not something to use during performance. 

The same goes for tools such as apps for writing or note taking. They all require their own level of skill that needs to be performed with certain minimal level of fluency and accuracy. Much of the time people just achieve those after a few repeats. But if you find, that you can only do practice or work at a certain time and place, practice doing it at different times. For general, people underestimate how much better their other work could be, if they practiced to use their tools a bit more.

### **Intentionality**

One last thing that will make repetition more powerful is intentionality. You are practicing with the intention of improving your performance. You are not doing it for the sake of practice. You are not doing it just as a random mindless repetition during every day activity.

You are introducing a certain amount of intentionality just by calling it practice. But you can do even more. Think explicitly about what your repetition is doing to improve your mental schemas. Focus on that and evaluate it from that perspective. You may think of it as a special kind of visualisation (meta visualisation).

Intentionality is also another way of introducing focus and attention into your practice. Those are both really important but they take a lot of effort and not-everybody finds that easy. By doing something with the intention of improving your working memory, you will find that you are more mindful of how distractions interfere with that.

One way to help intentionality is to set a timer and log what you are doing. That simple action tells your body that this is about something different. People still do get distracted and this is something that you may need to practice. But it is worth it. Tell yourself that you will not look at email, turn on music, go get a cup of coffee, during the time the timer is running (anywhere between 5 and 50 minutes). And practice how long you can do it. Make setting the timer a part of the ritual - a trigger for intentional, focused work.

You can even introduce intentionality into your regular practice. Just pause sometimes, redo an action you just did while thinking about how you could do it slightly better. Repeat it once more to see, if you change made a difference.

sections.title: Techniques for Reflection
sections.content:
# Four techniques for reflection to gather feedback

## Reflection and feedback gathering methods

Reflection is the necessary companion to repetition. Without reflection and deliberation, the time you spend repeating to practice is mostly wasted. But you must not just ponder, your reflection should aim to examine the feedback you got from the result of your performance. 

You should be reflecting on how your practice contributes to your performance and how it could improve further. You are practicing to improve, not to practice. Here are some techniques you can use:

1. Introspection
2. Diary or log
3. Comparison
4. Discussion

## **1 Introspection**

The easiest method is introspection. Simply examine your performance in your mind. You can do systematically or randomly. You will find that the people who are good at something are thinking about it much of their time. The people at the top of their game probably think of little else. They think about their progress, what they could do to improve, reflect on what they did, etc. 

If you find yourself thinking a lot about writing or language or whatever you are doing, this may be all the introspection you need. But most people need to be more systematic. Schedule time during each practice to think about how it went. Do think you have finished until you have reflected on the quality of what you did and what to do next. 

And if you remember during odd moments, think about how you are progressing and how your practice is doing overall. But do not think in general terms, try to be as specific as possible. Try to plan what you are going to practice next time.

But introspection has the same limits of working memory as everything. There’s only so much you can keep in your head. That’s when you need to introduce record keeping.

## **2 Diary or log**

Keeping a log is essential for tracking progress but it is also useful to keep a diary with more detailed thoughts or plans. 

This could be very simple - write down what you did, how it went and what you will do next time. This may take some effort but it is worth it. Just like with writing itself, you will discover things you did not know about yourself by having to formulate them in writing - even if it is just bullet points. 

During the process you will discover how easy it is to forget what you did even just a short time ago. You can use this opportunity to slow down, replay your practice in your mind and take note of what it was like. This will be an incredibly useful method of improving your ability to perceive how well you are doing. The process of writing it out explicitly will show you how many things you left unexamined.

## **3 Comparison or benchmarking**

No matter what you are doing, there’s a good chance others are doing it, as well. You can use what they are doing as a benchmark - both practically and emotionally. It is almost certain that almost anything someone you know or know about can do, you can do also. Maybe not exactly the same way or to the same degree but at least a little bit.

The trick is to find someone who is just a little bit better than you and compare what you are doing to them. They are your benchmark of what is possible. Your aim is not to beat them or show them up. Your aim is to calibrate your expectation. Your mantra should be:

> If many people can do something well that I struggle with, I can probably practice to get better at it. It is much more likely that I just haven’t figured out how to practice it than “I am not good at it”.
> 

This applies to everything. Running, driving, drawing, playing a musical instrument, doing math, speaking a foreign language, and of course, academic writing. 

In many fields, you cannot compare yourself to the top performers - runners, chess players, musicians. At that level you need to combine enormous amounts of practice with some natural predisposition (or at least a specific life story that enabled them to start early enough). But there are always enough people who are just above you, whose level you can reach.

But with other fields, there is no easy notion of ‘the best’.  This is most true of language in general and writing in particular. There is no reason why should not be able to compose any sentence or paragraph that anyone else can.  And that you should not be able to do it quickly enough to compose just as good a paper or essay as them. You may vary in speed and total volume of output but that does not matter, the basic stuff of performance is well within your reach. 

So the trick is to look at what those people are doing and think about what they did and then practicing to get to a point where you can replicate it. This is very easy with writing, because it is there in front of you and does not change.

A really good way to do benchmarking is to review the work of others in a group. This is something you can do with other people on the learning journey or, if you don’t know anybody, you can read reviews or watch videos assessing other people’s performance. This is available for music, photography, writing, many sports.

## **4 Discussion: Coaching and the limits to reflection**

There are limits to the amount of reflection you can do on your own. At the earliest stages, you don’t  yet have enough ability to perceive all aspects of what you are doing. This is when it helps to work with a coach. 

When we say the word “coach” we imagine someone who tells you what to do. But that is wrong. If that was all coaches did, we could learn from a step by step guide. In fact, the reason Couch to 5K works so reliably is because anybody following those steps can get those gains.

No, the reason to have a coach is to have someone to help you with reflection. Everything else a coach does such as setting out a programme or motivating you is just a bonus. You can mostly get those things for yourself with the help of textbooks of instructional videos. What you cannot get is that external perception of what you are doing. Even when you record yourself, you are not quite at the level where you can perceive all the problems. You can bootstrap your way to this level but a coach is a great shortcut.

You don’t always have somebody called ‘coach’ in your field. For example, there are writing coaches but they are few and far between. But you can always use a ‘teacher’ as a coach, too. Even in a class situation. Don’t go to class waiting for the teacher to tell you what to do and what to learn. Go there to get feedback on your performance. Do all the exercises and more and listen carefully to what the teacher tells you. They may not even realise that they are coaching you. 

Or you can always find somebody who is just a little better than you or even at the same level as you to give you feedback as an input into your reflection. The feedback can even be wrong and still be useful for reflection. Remember,  you are using a coach as a source of improved self-reflection to help you achieve more productive repetition. They cannot do the repetition for you and they cannot do the reflection for you, either. But they can be a great catalyst or accelerator. 

And finally, a coach, a teacher or even a class can give structure to your practice. People often complain about their teachers or classes. They say things like - ‘the teacher didn’t teach me what I need’ or ‘I never learn anything in class’. You can turn any class into a personal coaching session just by changing your perspective. This is a time to help you reflect on your practice and performance.
