# Dealing with emotions: Finding joy in boring practice

## What does practice feel like - finding joy in the “grind”

Practice and the learning associated with it is not just a mechanical step by step process. It is also an emotional process. And being able to expect, deal with and even manage the emotional load is as important as managing the cognitive load.

There are broadly two sources of emotions associated with practice:

1. Feelings about progress and skill level 
2. Feelings during and about the practice activities

These are often intertwined but it is useful to think of them separately.

## Progress curve emotional rollercoaster

Being good at something is not just something that happens. We grow a skill almost like another limb. It becomes a part of us, our identity and most importantly our comfort zone. Pushing outside of that comfort zone is by definition uncomfortable. 

We feel emotions when we enter a new field and we feel emotions when we try to improve. 

### **Beginner shock**

It is no fun to be a beginner. You may enjoy the novelty of learning something new for a while but soon you will start to feel like a foreigner lost in a far away land without a guide. Nothing makes sense, you feel like a child or you may start even questioning your own self worth.

Many of the emotions people go as they try to acquire a new skill or move to the next level are very similar to what people go through with culture shock. They not only feel bad, they feel physically and mentally tired, they withdraw and they may even develop a hatred of the new thing. 

This may sound extreme, but many people who gave up something often did it because it did not make them feel good about themselves. The initial excitement wore off and all that remained was drudgery. The difference between those who succeeded and those who gave up is that those who succeeded found a way to cope with the negative emotions and in the best case found a way to enjoy the process practice.

Here the lesson is: 

<aside>
🗒️ Practice hard early on so that you move out of the beginner stage and things start making more sense and you feel more at home

</aside>

### **Plateau comfort and regression stress**

Reaching a plateau is another source of negative feelings. The most common strategy for coping with this is that people think there’s no room to improve. They reached a sufficient level and they do not need to improve. This is probably true for most things in life - we can only improve at so many things. But it is not true in absolute terms. We can always improve at anything we do in one way or another. Even people at the top of their game (or perhaps especially those people) are always looking for ways to improve.

But another thing that happens is even more important and frequent source of why people don’t like leaving the comfort zones of their plateaus is that the first thing that happens as you try to improve some aspect of your performance is that you first get worse at it.

Sometimes this is obvious. For example, I would like to improve my typing by using a more efficient control of the keys. What will happen when I embark on a learning programme - my typing speed will decrease. I am happy with my typing speed - the main reason I want to type more efficiently is to reduce stress on my hands - so I don’t want to go through the pain. The immediate gain is too removed and the work involved too extensive.

But I will take the time to learn keyboard shortcuts of any new application I’m using because I know the benefit is huge and I have a good system for learning them, so the cost of time and effort is small. Many people find that too much work and will forego the benefit.

But sometimes the regression is hidden. I’m experiencing a change to my routines and I am starting to perceive the limits of my current performance. This causes more general tiredness and stress - so my performance suffers as a result in the short term - or very often the perceived effort of anything I do increases and I feel like my performance is less even when it is improving on any objective measure. That’s one of the reasons logging and keeping track of feedback is so important.

## Practice activities or Love the grind

<aside>
📎 “Enjoyment is a trainable skill.” — Thomas Basboll

</aside>

The most important thing to know about effective practice is that it mostly is not inherently enjoyable. In fact, not only is it not enjoyable, it can be emotionally draining and dispiriting as we saw above. When we talk about learning being fun, we are often talking about motivation. But the process of learning cannot be all fun.

Repeating something over and over while focusing on doing it as best as possible does not sound like fun because it is not. But it is possible to find enjoyment in it. Many people say they enjoy the pain of exercise because they know it is helping, they know they will feel better after, they like the structure it gives their life, or because they found joy in the moment.

Those who are lucky enough to find the joy on their own will be more likely to succeed. But that joy can be trained with reflection. Many of us did not start by liking coffee or wine but ‘developed a taste for it’. This was not by accident. We saw people enjoying these things and tried to replicate it. And most people succeeded in this. The same can be done with practice.

One surprisingly powerful way to develop enjoyment is mantras - short statements you develop and repeat to yourself while you are performing the activity. It could be as simply as saying to yourself “I’m enjoying this” or “this is getting better”. Many athletes use mantras during performance as a way of focusing and overcoming issues.  One of the strategies they use, is prepare and practice their mantras ahead of time to get used to them and try them in context. Yes, even mantras can be practiced and improved.

<aside>
🗒️ “Love the grind” Phily Bowden, elite runner and YouTuber

</aside>

Repeating a mantra to yourself while writing or speaking would not always be helpful, but you can use them when you are tired or don’t feel like getting started. They don’t have to be words. They can be images or sounds you bring up in your head. Different people have different things that work for them, don’t feel like you have to use exactly the same thing - try what works for you (and, yes, practice it).

## Studying vs practicing

Another insight on the question of practice and emotion comes from a surprising place - speed cubing. T Perm a champion speed cuber who makes instructional videos on speed cubing on YouTube observed that he sees two types of players with different preferences [REF]:

1. **Studying:** Learning new and new ways of doing something
2. **Practicing:** Repeating existing ways and getting really good at them

He associated the former with older players and the latter with older ones. His claim is that  practicing is usually more successful because if you only study without practice, you never develop the speed you need. Those who study new algorithms in speed cubing ignore aspects like improving their finger position on those they already know, or speed of recognition of existing patterns. 

Both are necessary to success but without practice, the studying is not enough. This was echoed by a teacher of bluegrass [REF] who observed a similar distinction in musicians and pointed out that this difference has an emotional dimension. Some people are more comfortable learning new concepts and find the ‘grind’ of repeating and improving one thing too tedious. But they end up with a large musical vocabulary they cannot use.

While this is not intrinsically linked to age, we can see that the older and more removed from the school age, the less we would be inclined to repeat something over and over. The sort of repetition that is required for successful practice just pushes us too far out of our emotional comfort zone.

## Benchmarking emotions and practice

Most of the time we only see expert performers at their best where we see them perform activities that seem far outside of what is imaginable for us. They make it look easy. We often admire them for the ease with which they seemingly do what they do.

But we are confusing ease for fluency. Fluency is not easy, it takes a lot of work. Luckily, in the age of YouTube and podcasts we have much more access to the experiences of elite performers as they share what they do and how with the rest of the world. And the message is clear: they suffer, they have doubts, they get tired, they hit plateaus.

We understand that they have to put in hours of practice but never consider how they feel during it. This is important. Your feelings while you are learning are the most likely reason you won’t practice. You may supress them by avoiding it altogether or you will be surprised by them and think you are doing something wrong.

It is important to benchmark your emotions - find out about what people in your field say, take it seriously when they talk about feelings. Here’s a personal example.

Most people would consider me good at learning foreign languages. I can usually get to a a very basic conversational level after a few weeks that seems to take many people a few months. People say things ‘you have a good memory’ or ‘you are good at languages’. That is not true at all. I have figured out a way to practice a language in context (using many of the techniques above). I am confident that I can do this with any language given enough incentive. However, it is a painful process. To help others understand it, I once kept a diary of the first two months of my learning Albanian [REF] and you can see how painful and frustrating the process was. I was not as deliberate about it as I could have been but the difference between me and others around me was that I was doing the work and I’d had the confidence that it would work out. The reason I kept the diary was to set a benchmark for what is possible but more important what it feels like. The message was, learning can be done even by somebody who actually does not have a good memory or (as my school teachers can attest), is not good at studying languages. They were not always feeling positive. 

So, if you are feeling negative emotions during the learning process, you can be confident that others are feeling the same.

# Deliberate practice as a way of overcoming limitations of working memory
Draft outline of a theory of deliberate practice by Dominik Lukeš.
### Deliberate practice background Deliberate practice has gained a lot of attention recently as a way of developing and improving expert performance without reference to innate predispositions such as talent. Of course, certain innate as well as environmental predispositions will play a role, particularly when it comes to the differentiation of performance at the very peak. The height of basketball players is often given as example [ref]. However, the key lesson of deliberate practice is that the lack of talent or merely not being naturally "good at" something does not prevent someone from achieving a significant level of competence. Deliberate practice has been the subject of many popular books, as well as academic treatments [ref] and was summarised by its originator Anders Ericsson in Peak [ref]. However, many of these books and countless articles and blogposts focus on the process. They emphasise things like getting feedback, working with coaches, breaking tasks into smaller components, working in short focused spurts. And that is all good advice. However, it ignores what I believe is the main and most **revolutionary contribution of deliberate practice**. Namely, redefining the goal of skill acquisition as the building of mental representations in order to overcome the universal limitations of working memory. ### Mental representations and chunks What are mental representations? Most simply mental representations are chunks that can be held in working memory and with which we can perform operations in order to achieve the task. Or in other words, articulate our intent. The idea goes back to GA Miller's seminal paper from 1956 "The Magical Number Seven Plus or Minus 2". In it., Miller talks about what appears to be fundamental limit of working (or in his words "immediate") memory in that it can only hold approximately 7 pieces of information. The precise number has been debated over the years [ref] but the fact that a small finite limit exists is beyond doubt. However, and this is where Miller's and Ericsson's insights merge, is that there does not seem to be any meaningful limit to the size of these pieces. They are not bits of information but rather chunks, or in Ericsson's terms "mental representations". Both chunks and mental representations are terminologically laden and subject to confusion across various research traditions. I will use them interchangeably simply to mean pieces of mental or physical performance that can be held in working memory in such a way that they can be manipulated without need for further articulation. To give trivial examples. To express the plural of the word "dog", we need to add the suffix "s" which is furthermore pronounced /z/ due to the coarticulation with the preceding consonant. All of those components need to be successfully articulated. Yet, the only demand of saying 'dogs' on working memory is topronounce /dogz/. We could go through the same step by step analysis of an entire sentence such as "The dogs are barking." where not only do we need to produce this articulation for each individual word and also their interaction and that of the sentence as a whole. But all that is required of working memory is to deal with a unitary chunk. The sentence "the dogs are barking". The same applies to primarily physical tasks such as driving. Shifting gears consists of a number of physical steps but the driver is only minimally competent when she can perform them as one. The process is then incorporated into the process of turning and slowing down which includes changing gears and its many subarticulations but also assessing the situation, turning the wheel, etc. ### Mental representations and expertise What sets apart experts from lay performers is the size of the chunks upon which they can confidently operate. For example a racecar driver, can perform all of the actions involved in shifting gears while turning under conditions of stress. All this at high speed while paying attention to her competitors, instructions from the navigator and while planning manoeuvres, several hundred or even thousand meters hence. A sports commentator can produce a continuous flow of relevant and coherent speech for extended periods of time while paying attention to what goes on on the field, technical aspects of the broadcasting equipment and instructions from the production team [ref Goffman]. Yet, when these and other experts' working memory is tested, they are not found to exceed the limitations identified by Miller [ref]. It is not only the raw size of the mental representations but also their richness. For instance, mnemonic devices are often used to facilitate recall. What this means that one has to remember more things in order to learn something simpler. Memory champions often focus on creating rich associations to facilitate memory, thus increasing the richness of the chunks they hold in working memory without increasing the demands on memory capacity. [ref - Moonwalking with Einstein] This also explains why there are limits to the transferrability of expertise between different domains or sometimes even different situations [ref]. The mental representations, in order to be useful for their primary task of reducing the working memory load, must be richly embedded in their environment which in turn also introduces new demands on working memory. For instance, public performances of music require additional practice compared to solitary playing. Equally, any foreign language learner will have experienced the notion of being tongue tied when faced with a real situation, even using language that they acquired perfectly in the classroom [ref Goin in Brown]. Practice therefore needs to be focused on the performance of the skill in real context. We can also use this phenomenon to explain why teaching to the test works and fails to produce actual skill without additional focus. ### Deliberate practice as method Deliberate practice can then be best understood as a method for increasing the size and richness of mental representations or chunks in a particular domain of expertise. However, the realization that this is the goal of practice, and then learning how to identify the next mental representations to develop are just as important as the techniques associated with the process of practice, if not more. Without chunks or mental representations as the clear goal, deliberate practice can devolve into meaningless repetition. What then is the nature of deliberate practice? First, Ericsson [ref] differentiates between purposeful practice and deliberate practice. However, his use of the terms is inconsistent [ref] and for the sake of simplicity, I will use deliberate practice to include activities that are primarily characteristics of purposeful practice which Ericsson sees as being more effective than pure repetition but less effective than full deliberate practice. However, when trying to apply deliberate practice to areas outside its original scope, these fine distinction would be more detrimental than beneficial. It is important to keep in mind that such differentiation exists when exploring the concept further. The key characteristic of deliberate practice is focused repetition of performing the component of a skill in question. The success depends on timely feedback and guidance from a coach. The feedback needs to lead to a revision of the performance as well as the reassessment of the desired building blocks of the skill. Deliberate practice is most likely to be successful if the learner follows an established programme of study supported by an experienced coach who exceeds the learner's level of competence. The role of the coach is important in order to increase effectiveness of the practice in that the coach can provide feedback and suggest ways of correcting performance. This is essential at the peak levels of expert performance where any improvement is going to be small and require extreme focus and effort to achieve. Since the concept of deliberate practice came at least in part out of research of elite performers, the focus on coaching and training programmes is a big part of the literature. However, in order to make deliberate practice accessible in non-elite, less resources contexts, it is essential that alternatives to coaching be identified. The literature suggests a number of approaches. Peer coaching and feedback has been shown to be particularly effective. However, using automated feedback instruments - for instance, music or language apps - can also serve to provide actionable feedback. The learner can also benefit from recording their performance (music, physical activities, foreign language) or keeping track of measurable aspects of performance where recording is not practicable (number of errors, time, routine maintenance). Finally, significant performance improvements can also be gained simply by following an established routine. Here, the famous example is the Couch to 5K running programmes that can take most beginners from no ability to run to being able to run 5 kilometres in approximately 8 weeks. There is no one established description of the steps of deliberate practice but for the purposes of further discussion, we can summarise it as follows. 1. Identify performance target and the mental representations or chunks required for performance within the limits of working memory. At some levels, this may only be possible with the help of a coach or a teacher. The performance target also needs to be frequently revised as intermediate stages are reached and the learners ability to perceive their own performance changes. 2. Identify components of mental representations (levels of performance) to provide target for practice. This may include scaffolding, i.e. practicing skills required for the acquisition of the skill rather than the skill itself (for instance acquiring a metalanguage, ability to count time in music, or developing a practice routine). In skills, where performance is not immediately susceptible to measurement, identify measurable aspects of performance or a way of recording progress in order to receive feedback. 3. Practice component chunks in a focused way until their component actions stop requiring individual attention. This requires repetition with close focus on small details of performance. The level of focus required means that this level of practice cannot be sustained for long periods and can only be effective if performed regularly in relatively small chunks of 30-60 minutes. Practice should always be slightly above the current level of skill. Ideally, at the level where the learner can perceive the target performance. The actual practice techniques will vary by the target performance, the current skill level and interest of the individual. In most areas, there are likely to be many different practice techniques that can lead to successful acquisition of the required mental representations. 4. Measure progress regularly by reviewing when multistep-actions become single performance chunks. This step may require some creativity in areas not naturally susceptible to measurement. Some areas, such as sport and musical performance have established assessment metrics. In sport, aspects of performance such as speed, distance or weight are not only inherently measurable but also can form the target for improvement. However, in most areas any measurement will only be a proxy for progress. It is essential to avoid the trap of confusing the measure with the target performance. The only true measure of progress is the ability to perform operations on the acquired mental representations in working memory as single chunks. Where this is not susceptible to external observation or reflected in a measurement proxy, introspection will be required of the learner. 5. Review target mental representations and identify non-performance scaffolding chunks. One of the most common mistakes is to confuse the performance target with certain stages required to achieve it. For instance, acquiring metalanguage or other metacognitive apparatus is necessary to be able to effectively monitor progress or identify areas to focus on. However, that is rarely part of the performance itself. For instance, memorising vocabulary is an essential part of learning a language. However, recalling words in response to a prompt is a separate performance to speaking a language. Fluent speakers do not 'recall' words, they use them to achieve their communicative goals. It is therefore always essential to focus on the context of performance. ### Identifying and monitoring mental representations On this account of deliberate practice, identifying and monitoring mental representations is essential to learning. However, no systematic study has been done of mental representations across various areas. There is not even a coherent theoretical account of mental representations. In fact, even research on working memory building on Miller's initial insight has mostly stalled [ref]. The identification of the mental representations has mostly been left to practitioners. The target mental representations are often left implicit in the practice guides or didactic manuals. However, it would appear that any one performance level can be achieved via different progress routes and any skill can be broken down into different chunks for successful performance. There are obvious limits to the variability but it is not necessary to assume that all learners need to follow identical paths or even focus on exactly the same chunks as targets for practice. This is most important when considering the starting point for any activity. ### Transfer of mental representations across tasks As hinted, mental representations or chunks only transfer in a limited way across domains. The transfer only happens if two different performances of a task share a similar articulation. The mental representation required for fluent spelling or basic grammatical structures such as agreement or basic morphology transfer across all writing tasks. However, going from writing down sentences to fluently composing a coherent paragraph of academic English is an entirely independent journey of acquiring mental representations. But even at that level, different genres or contexts will require different mental representations. Academics find it notoriously difficult to write for the general public. That is because the chunks built up to write an academic papers are unsuitable for the press. And new chunks have to be developed. Both tasks are articulated through a certain level of syntactic complexity that makes the transfer easier but ultimately, the process is akin to learning a foreign language. This same issue is present across all domains of expertise. Chess players cannot just pick up Go and succeed. Medical diagnosticians cannot easily diagnose difficulties with their computers. Even though in both cases, the abstract principles that emerge when the task is described as a feat of reason are almost identical. Yet, the mental representations required to actually perform the reasoning within the limits of working memory make the transfer almost impossible. This could also explain why generalist managers so often struggle across significantly different domains. While in practice there are both successes and failures [ref], the successes can only be possible if the manager develops sufficient fluency about their new field. But equally, this explains why domain experts frequently make inadequate managers. While they can easily conceptualise the set of actions required for success, they never acquired mental representations to reason with sufficient fluency about the process through which they can be achieved. The lesson is that the primary focus of any practice should be acquiring mental representations for the task at hand. And as we saw above, successfully identifying the task and the requisite mental representations is a key component of successful deliberate practice ### Mental representations and perception From the above, it is clear that mental representations also have an impact on perception. Experts can not only produce and operate with larger chunks, they can also perceive larger chunks. An expert can see at a glance a complex situation and identify the problem whereas a novice needs to decode their world step by step, in a manner much more similar to a computer algorithm. For instance, a master chess player will see a very complex board configuration and immediately see the outcome without having to consider individual configuration of pieces. Concert musicians frequently see entire sections of a complex score as simply one element whereas a novice would have to decode every individual note. This is, of course, trivially true of reading and writing at the lower levels of articulation. Obviously, expert readers can operate at higher speed and focus on more aspects of text other than simply the decoding of sequences of letters into mental images of words or their aural representations. However, expert readers of academic literature can pay attention to many more aspects of the text, they can skim, scan and make judgements at a glance. An expert reader of academic literature will also see be able to make connections, understand contexts and make more informed decisions about which parts of text to pay special attention to. This is also relevant to the writing process since a more expert reader will be able to better edit their own writing. Although it needs to be pointed out that the task of editing and test revision is different from reading for content and the transfer is not complete. However, some level of expertise in reading a text in a specific genre will be required for editing. The same applies even in more complex areas such as medical diagnostics, emergency response, strategy, teaching, management, however, it has not been studied much outside of medical diagnostic fields and surgery. It is important to note the great controversy around the impact of mental representations on perception. However, the claim here is not that the expert is "literally" seeing or hearing something different than the non-expert. The expert merely requires less time and fewer steps to process the relevant information whereas a novice will require so much time and so many step that their working memory will be effectively swamped and the effect will be some species of "attentional blindness". [ref] ### Mental representations and automaticity This requires an important caveat. What I have been describing could lead us to assume that the goal of deliberate practice is automaticity. The ability to perform tasks without thinking about them. This might be reminiscent of the famous distinction between levels of competence based on meta-cognition or awareness: Unconscious Incompetence, Conscious Incompetence, Conscious Competence, Unconscious Competence. It might appear, that deliberate is a process of achieving unconscious competence. But nothing could be further from the truth. It is true that some levels of articulation form mental representations that are beyond the scope of conscious notice [ref Talmy]. For instance, articulation of phonemes in fluent speech is an example of competence that is not only unconscious but cannot be made conscious by an expert speaker without explicit training. However, almost any effort through which we might want to acquire mental representations will not focus on articulations of this kind. While it is not based on research or theory [ref], this framework makes intuitive sense and is frequently deployed in training. The assumption is that unconscious competence is the target of instruction. It bears noting that in the original conception of this metaphor, this was not the case. It was first used to describe missionary educators and those with conscious competence were given as the examples of more effective practitioners [ref]. But true expertise requires a much more nuanced perspective that can be guided by the focus on the limitations of working memory. In order to be able to reason and act in a sufficiently fluent manner, the expert cannot consciously attend to all the component mental representations required to perform the action. And as noted, at lower levels of articulation, this is impossible. However, this does not mean that the chunks or mental representations have become opaque monads to them. They can still make parts of their articulated structure available for inspection while attending to their use. The structure of the chunk and the chunk itself create a larger chunk which can be operated on in working memory. In short, experts do not perform actions automatically without thinking, they perform them deliberately while using larger and richer chunks. To an outside observer, it may appear effortless or almost extrasensory in terms of perception. And experts frequently describe themselves thus. But when the expert performance is analysed, the structure and use of mental representations become much clearer. In short, the expert needs to both have access to the structure of their mental representations and operate on them as if they were monadic units. ### Practice, enjoyment and motivation The final consideration for deliberate practice is that it is unlikely to be inherently enjoyable due to the level of focus required. This is made worse by the fact that the particular thing practiced may not be directly meaningful and only serve as a scaffold. For instance, repeating scales in different patterns does not feel like playing music, or memorising vocabulary does not seem like speaking a language. Ericsson reports that successful practitioners learn to find enjoyment in the process, particularly with respect to the progress. Given the amount of effort required, maintaining motivation is essential. Again, there is no definitive prescription for this but the most common suggestion is to monitor progress and reassess goals in order to receive perceptible performance rewards. This can develop a positive feedback loop, since monitoring progress is essential to the process of deliberate practice. However, there is also a danger of circularity. It is a common side effect of gamification where the goal of obtaining the performance reward supersedes that of learning. For instance, learners using gamified vocabulary apps may focus on achieving high scores and optimise the process for achieving those as opposed for building a repository of words they can use. The measurement of progress must include a reflection of how the change in skill contributes to the ultimate goal of building larger chunks. It is important that learners find ways to make repeated focused practice not just bearable but also enjoyable. This can include various rewards and varying the practice routine. Practicing in different tempos, with and without background music, etc. can reduce some of the tedium of the repetition required. But ultimately, the main source of enjoyment needs to be from the fact that the practice leads to improvement on the journey to the final goal. Seeing the results of practice in actual performance will be the greatest motivator. To paraphrase the virtuoso bassist Victor Wooten from an interview he gave on stage: > Don't think about how bad you feel now when it seems like you will never get it. Think about how great you'll feel next week, when you'll be able to do this. > The importance of this for writing was stated most clearly by Basboll [ref] who suggests that finding enjoyment in the act of writing should be one of the goals of the process of practice. In his words, "enjoyment is a trainable skill". This can be achieved by periodic reflection on the benefits of the "writing moment", the focused time when writing or writing practice is the main focus. ### Variability in effects of repetition and aptitude One of the commonly recognised realities of instruction is the variability in how individuals respond to the same instruction across different subjects. Some people seemingly develop mental representations in certain fields by mere repetition, sometimes without any outward effort. First, we know that that some chunks and mental representations do develop simply by repetition in almost anyone engaging in them repeatedly. Any typist will improve their speed over time, an adult studying a foreign language will acquire new words, beginner drivers will improve over time in how they navigate traffic and handle the vehicle. Sometimes a few repetitions suffice to develop a sufficient mental representation. When a person moves into a new home, they will go through a period of small adjustments. Initially, even turning the lights on or opening doors requires conscious effort. Yet, in a matter of days of weeks, one develops sufficient "fluency" in performing these actions that they become automatic. Instead of looking for the light switch, thinking about which light it turns on, which way the toggle goes to turn it on, the action of switching on the light is one thing. I walk into a room with the intention of turning the light on and my body will perform the action of turning the light on as if it were one. Repetition over time was all that was necessary, although the process will involve some amount of conscious reflection. However, mere repetition is not sufficient to overcome the inevitable performance plateaus. After reaching a plateau, performance stops improving or may even degrade over time. But perhaps even more importantly, individuals will differ in their ability to build mental representations in a given field by mere repetition. This is perhaps what can best be described as aptitude or talent. While the basic tenet of deliberate practice is that within certain limits no general human skill is outside the reach of anyone engaging in practice aimed at developing mental representations, it would be hard to deny that individuals differ. For instance, the development of reading or writing skills at all levels displays a large degree of variability across all levels from primary school to academic writing. Individuals exposed to by and large the same instruction develop differently. However, most people develop sufficient reading and writing skills through instruction that is primarily conceptual followed by procedural repetition with no focus on building mental representations. Yet, the requisite mental representations do develop in a large proportion of the population. But equally a significant minority will never develop sufficient fluency in reading and an even larger proportion will never become fluent writers. The disparity is even higher in analogous procedural skills such as mathematics or foreign languages, or even physical activities such as sports or musical performance. What accounts for this variability is a matter of speculation but traditionally it has been ascribed to aptitude or talent. In reading and writing, often the disparity is a result of specific cognitive impairments such as dyslexia or SLI. However, even these limitations can be overcome with a structured approach to instruction where mental representations are cumulatively built up under the careful supervision of the teacher acting as coach. In cases, where the variability cannot be explained by recognisable cognitive or physical limitations, the differences may be attributed to a difference in how repetition is engaged in by the individual in the given subject. Most likely explanation is a positive feedback loop between initial success of building the foundational mental representations leading to the accessibility of further practice. These individuals are more likely to engage in more reflection about the process which further enhances what may be externally perceived as mere practice through repetition. This is important for developing academic or non-academic writing skills. Words such as talented writer are often used to talk about certain individuals. Yet, this often ignores the amount of reflection these individuals engage in in their practice and how it increase the amount of repetition which further develops these skills. Struggling writers will need to be reminded of this fact. ### Time required for developing mental representations Another issue not sufficiently addressed in the literature is the time required to convert component actions into chunks that can be operated on by working memory. The total number of 10,000 hours has been suggested [ref] as the typical amount of time required to achieve peak performance levels in certain fields. Ericsson suggests it takes multiple years, as many as 10, during which deliberate practice is the main focus, to achieve peak performance skill. This is clearly not realistic advice for most instances because it only focuses on peak performers and does not consider the fact that most people only need to develop a skill to a much lower level of performance in order for it to become useful for their aims. However, no evidence-based guidelines exist for the amount of time required to develop such useful and usable mental representations. But we can turn to an estimate by Josh Kaufman [ref] who suggests that it takes 20 hours to develop basic mental representations in a field of effort. He presents several case studies of personal development where 20 hours over the course of about 4-6 weeks helped him develop usable skills in a domain. For instance, he reports learning to play four chords on a ukulele, learn yoga to improve his mobility, learn basics of a new programming language, and learn to type using a new keyboard layout. While no research exists to confirm this estimate, we can triangulate this approximate time span by comparing similar instructional programmes. For instance, the famous running programme Couch to 5k (C25K) succeeds in developing running skills over the course of 9 weeks and a total of about 15 hours of practice. A summer school in a foreign language may offer students about 30 hours of meaningful practice over the course of two weeks. The Writing Process Reengineering programme discussed below is designed to run over 8 weeks with a total starting at about 20 hours. 20 hours over 8 weeks is also the approximate amount of instruction received by students in an academic subject over the course of a semester. As a broad estimate, we that anyone engaging in 15 - 40 hours of deliberate practice over the course of 2 to 10 weeks can develop sufficient combination mental representations or chunks that can be operated on in working memory in order to allow them to legitimately perform in a field albeit where they previously had no competence at all. This performance will be significantly limited and it will take many repetitions of these learning sprints to achieve even moderate levels of expert performance. However, this gives a realistic estimate on the lower bound of time for deliberate practice. This can then be transformed into usable programmes for developing academic writing skills or other analogous procedural skills.

sections.title: Metaphors of Writing
sections.content:
# Metaphors of Writing for Deliberate Practice

### Writing as a foreign language

From the perspective of a novice writer, writing is effectively a foreign language [ref Jim Miller, genre research]. The conventions and structures of the written language often effectively constitute a different language, not only at the level of vocabulary or syntax but even at the level of type [ref]. For instance, the type of nominalisation common in academic and bureaucratic language is reminiscent of the difference between incorporating and non-incorporating languages [ref Haspelmath].  

This is further underscored when we realise that, it is possible for non-native speakers to write quite fluently in an academic register without being able to demonstrate anywhere near the level of idiomatic fluency in daily conversation. 

The main difference between writing and learning a foreign language is that the native speaker learning to produce written language is not building their linguistic representations from scratch and can therefore draw on existing chunks of articulation. However, as Dabrowska demonstrated [ref], there are clear limits to how native speakers can deal with written language of increasing complexity. Learning to write clearly requires reading to construct quite different chunks of language than learning to speak. For many writers, this happens naturally through repetition but others require more targeted practice.

What this means for writing is that the identification of mental representations will be similar to that when learning a foreign language. And indeed most academic writing guides focus on this almost to the exclusion of anything else. They provide lists of words, phrases and constructions to be acquired very much like a foreign language [ref - examples].  Equally, Academic English courses are often provided by the Language departments under the heading of EAP (English for Academic Purposes).

However, the question that remains largely unaddressed in writing, is the question of the communicative situation. The biggest challenge in foreign language instruction is to ensure that the learner can deploy the learned constructions at the moment of communication. This is both easier and harder with writing. Writing clearly does not impose the sort of time pressure with its concomitant imposition on the working memory. Unlike speaking, writing is not a irreversibly linear process. Indeed, it is often said that writing is in large part editing and rewriting. 

At the same time, however, writing requires working with much larger chunks and the development of many layers of mental representations. This makes it easy for the writing tutor to inadvertently skip levels of articulation, leaving the student behind in their needs. This seems to happen to weaker students in the PROCESS approach [ref - systematic review].  

### Writing as translation

> "we have all had the experience of uttering or writing a sentence, then stopping and realizing that it wasn't exactly what we meant to say. To have that feeling, there has to be a difference in what we meant to say from what we said." (Steven Pinker, Language Instinct)
> 

Writing is clearly more than just putting the down the contents of one's thoughts on paper. Writers report not fully realizing what it was that they meant until it was written down. And rereading ones own writing often causes writers a sense of disconnect, not dissimilar to first hearing their speech on a recording. Fluent writing, requires that a writer develops mental representations (dual constructions) that constitute pairs of patterns of thought and patterns of written expression.

In this sense, writing is a kind of translation. To explore the metaphor further, we can imagine two languages: "mentalese" and "writtenese" between which the writer has to learn to translate. As any translator knows, translation is not a matter of finding one-to-one correspondences between words but rather equivalents between entire chunks of expression. Not everything is equally amenable to translation. Idioms, cultural allusions, complex imagery, puns are just a few of the types of constructions that can only ever be translated in part. The translator has to constantly make choices between being faithful to the structure of the author's language or to the author's intention. Both require a certain degree of interpretation.

But perhaps the most difficult challenge in translation is when the structure of one language requires the writer to commit to a meaning which the other language leaves unexpressed. In that case, the translator literally has to fill in gaps and make commitments to meaning which the original author did not have to do. This can even reveal inconsistencies and gaps in the original text. This could happen even in the most innocuous seeming constructions. For instance, the definition of the level A1 in the Common European Frame of Reference for languages (CEFR) begins: "Can understand and use familiar everyday expressions". Yet, the construction "understand and use" needs to be broken up into multiple clauses in some languages which may completely change the emphasis. 

This is clearly very clearly reminiscent of the idea that writing is filling in gaps in ones thought. But at the same time some writers report that they find it relatively easy to write down the contents of their own thought. Some do it by rehearsing what they will write before setting it down,  some may visualise the text as written first. Yet, others train their thought processes to more closely hew to what is written. But some adjustment is required. 

This is one aspect of writing least susceptible to explicit instruction because it is impossible to give examples of the contents of somebody's mind without these having been processed through writing. However, there are parallels such as those between written and spoken language or two different languages. This can then help the student identify possible mental representations which can then be developed through deliberate practice. 

Thomas Basboll has also been exploring the related metaphor of writing as drawing, where the would be artist has to learn to perceive the world in a new way and pay attention to its aspects that will contribute to a visually communicative representation. This is reminiscent of the way in which translator must build up a reservoir of parallelisms between the two languages.

### Writing as a physical activity

Writing is without question a literal physical activity. It requires not just mental but also physical exertion. Handwriting or typing while seated or standing, require physical coordination as well as a certain degree of stamina. Even dictation has a physical component. But writing is also reminiscent of physical activity in other ways. It takes place over time in a physical space, it requires tools and equipment. It also requires focus and endurance. 

Each of these elements of the writing process place demands on the working memory to navigate successfully. At the moment of writing, the novice writer may struggle with being able to write in large enough chunks because they can only ever operationalise small chunks of writing due to the working memory being filled with the process of mechanics of writing. They are writing in words rather than sentences or paragraphs and the idea of generating coherent ideas through writing completely eludes them.

This is not dissimilar to novice runners who can only ever focus on the next minute or two of running in terms of planning their effort. Their run is articulated into much smaller segments than that of an expert runner. This has led to the development of techniques such as the famous Couch to 5K (C25K) which can transform a non-runner into a competent runner capable of running five kilometers in between 30 and 45 minutes. The process takes about 8-12 weeks and requires and begins with runs of 90 seconds, slowly building up to larger chunks.

This can serve as a model for the development of writing in ever increasing units. Going from phrases to sentences and paragraphs and ultimately to entire essays. We need to start with the acknowledgement that for the novice writer, the essay looms as much as the five-kilometer distance does for the non-runner. While the articulation of writing is in may ways more complex than that of running, the novice writer typically does not start without any linguistic background. It is not therefore inconceivable that a period similar to that of C25K could help a reluctant writer achieve greater fluency and stamina even while many aspects of writing expertise remain to be addressed through further practice.

Of course, another aspect of practice for physical activity is in person coaching where the coach gives feedback in real time. This seems much less applicable but at least one such framework exists:

> During one of these “writing with the teacher present” classes, a student said that these classes were more like athletic practice than class. We were practicing while the coach was around to break steps down into smaller and smaller elements and to help us learn the skills “in real time.”
> 

More below.

### Writing as a musical performance

The act of writing is both analogous and disanalogous  to music. The disanalogy is clear. Music performance is linear and its success depends on it being performed without technical flaws and with appropriate expressiveness without interruption. Writing, on the other hand, is circular requiring a number of recursive steps at every stage. Writing, rewriting, editing and reediting are commonly recognised as crucial elements of the writing process.

However, this is to overlook the fact, that a certain level of fluency is required in writing. The competent writer will indeed spend a significant amount of time redrafting, however, what matters is at which level of articulation the drafts and redrafts take place. When we observe the extremely dysfluent writer, for instance, young writers with dyslexia [ref], we see that the lack of fluency in constructing larger chunks prevents them from expressing their intentions. Writing then becomes an exercise in frutration.

The skills at all levels of articulation required for musical performance are analogous to those necessary for the composition of a viable draft, that can then be subject to rewriting and editing. Many elite musical performers have described the process of preparation for the performance of a new difficult piece. And their aim is universally to identify repeated patterns organised in large chunks that enable them to "think" ahead or "reason" about the piece, recover from stumbles and focus on expressiveness over the technical aspects. 

However, to achieve this level of expressive fluency, the musical performer has to spend a significant amount of time on focused repetition of patterns at lower levels of articulation. Practicing scales and arpeggios to "get a feel" for a particular key or chord progression on their instrument. 

Luckily, the amount of focused repetition is probably significantly lower for the novice writer because of the pre-existing mental representations that can be developed further. However, no empirical data on the difference exists. 

Unlike musical performers, who, by this stage, have been pre-selected for their aptitude, almost anybody is expected to be able to write. It is therefore important to think about other sources of continued dysfluencies despite focused repetition These could be as simple as lack of typing skills or as complex as dyslexia. However, the writer is much freer in their mode of expression and free to choose dictation or handwriting as appropriate.

## Writing as a skill subject to multiple articulation

Writing is a skill. And any skill can be improved. Simply doing more of it will help. However, there is a point after which mere repetition does not help. In fact, many skills tend to atrophy and may even  slightly decrease with pure repetition without any goal for improvement. [ref Medical diagnosticians]

Skills are not unitary monadic entities. They are complex, multifaceted, task and context-embedded and multiply articulated. It is this multiple articulation that will serve as a departure point here for integrating  deliberate practice into the writing process. The performance of any task is happening at multiple levels of articulation. The notion of articulation comes from the linguistic concept of dual articulation of language. While we are trying to articulate ideas when we speak, we also have to articulate the sounds that make up the words we are using. And we further have to shape the words into the right forms and the sentences into the right sequences. Which is also a form articulation. But speech would be impossible if we had to pay conscious attention to every aspect of its production. And that's why when  we say we are trying to articulate an idea, we do not mean any of the mechanical components of producing language.

The same notion of articulation applies to any skill, however. A runner does not have to nor can she pay attention to every aspect of her motion. She is trying to achieve a task distance, speed or merely exercise and articulates the completion of the task through running. But she does not articulate the run. A typist may have the task of speed, accuracy or simply transmission of knowledge. She will not focus on every aspect of the task. 

Even more complex skills such as driving or even medical diagnostics are subject to this multiple articulation. In order to achieve, express or articulate the task a driver or diagnostician must perform a myriad of other actions which are often further articulated. Yet, paying heed to all or any one of them would simply overwhelm the capacity of their working memory and preclude them from achieving the main goal. [cf. Miller and magical number 7]

The notion of multiple articulation applies even more directly to the process of writing. The writer's main goal is not to just write words down. It is to articulate ideas in such a way that will faithfully represent the writer's ideas and that will result in an understanding by the reader. Create images in the reader's mind [cf. Pinker]. But in order to achieve that ultimate articulation, multiple other articulations must happen. The writer must adopt a certain physical posture and perform movements with their fingers. She must choose, shape, and arrange words. Those words require spelling. The choice of words and their arrangement will be subject to genre, style and register.  It is only by being able to articulate all of these that the writer can achieve her task. That of articulating her ideas.

sections.title: Reviews of Writing Programs
sections.content:
# Reviews of writing coaching programmes

How can we reconceptualise writing instruction from the perspective of deliberate practice and multiple articulation? The good news is that many if not most writing programmes already include components that could be considered deliberate practice. What they appear to lack is a focus at building up larger mental representations at multiple levels of articulation.

There are very few academic writing programmes that take a structured approach to the development of writing skills. In this section, I will briefly consider the Process approach which has been gaining popularity and has generated some research evidence [ref] . I will then compare two structured approaches to coaching writing and will offer a suggestion for a possible programme based on insights from all three working towards the idea of building up larger mental representations. Unfortunately, this section will of necessity be speculative since there is little evidence base to draw on.

### Process

The most common approach to teaching writing is Process [ref Coffin et al 2013]. The focus on the process of writing is consonant with deliberate practice. However, there is no coherent programme of study associated with Process. It appears to consist of its main philosophy and an eclectic mix of instructional activities. Many of these activities would form a core part of any instructional programme but there is no sense of progression across levels of articulation. It is not surprising that a meta analysis [ref] showed only modest improvements overall and no improvement for struggling writers.

The one crucial element of the Process approach is it emphasis on early, actionable feedback. Feedback both by instructors and peers is essential for the development of writing skills. Here the process literature and wealth of practical knowledge provides an invaluable resource to anybody wanting to enhance their deliberate practice with more relevant feedback.

In short, it is without doubt that any deliberate practice schema will include a significant number of techniques from the process approach but these would need to be structured around an individualised course of progression as the developing writers continue to build up chunks of increasing size across multiple levels of articulation.

### Writing process reingineering - Basboll

The cumulative and habit based approach promoted by the writing coach Thomas Basbol is an eight-week programme that focuses on building writing habits but also on practicing the form of the paragraph built around a topic sentence.

The writer is advised to schedule a block of time (30 minutes) and commit to write and edit one paragraph during that time. To facilitate this, the writer should construct a topic sentence the evening before. 

For Basboll the paragraph is a foundational unit of academic writing and through this process, it is possible for writers to accumulate enough writing to become productive. 

The writing process reingineering assumes that all other writing skills are available and the writer has requisite fluency in writing academic language and writing in general. All that the programme offers is the development of stamina.

### Frameworks for Academic Writing - Poulter

[Book: Frameworks for Academic Writing (Poulter)](https://human.libretexts.org/Bookshelves/Composition/Advanced_Composition/Book%3A_Frameworks_for_Academic_Writing_(Poulter))

Frameworks for academic writing is very much based around the idea of building up chunks or mental representations at the various level of articulation of the writing process. It outlines patterns at the level of phrase, clause and paragraphs, and it encourages trainee writers to apply them to their own writing through practice. It very much goes beyond the simple 'academic English' paradigm by focusing on larger constructs but at the same time not simply limiting itself to genre forms such as essay or general compositional structures like the paragraph or topic sentence. Each component of the written whole is presented through a series of prompts from which templates are constructed illustrated by an example of use.

> **The point that** [*insert author’s last name*] **seems to be making in this** [*insert type of selection*] **is** [*insert what you think the message or point is here*].
> 

The words in bold provide the basic structure for the writing assignment while the parts in square brackets are expected to be replaced by the trainee writer's own words. It is important, that the amount of text the student is expected to write is on the order of words to sentences.

But what brings the Frameworks for Academic Writing even closer to the principles of deliberate practice is reframing the role of the writing teacher and the purpose of the writing sessions. The origin of the idea is described in the introduction:

> One breakthrough idea that emerged from listening to students was the request to have writing teachers present while drafting their papers. They wanted to do their drafting during class.
> 

This practice allowed the role of the teacher being framed as that of a coach:

> During one of these “writing with the teacher present” classes, a student said that these classes were more like athletic practice than class. We were practicing while the coach was around to break steps down into smaller and smaller elements and to help us learn the skills “in real time.”
> 

### POWER by Patricia Goodson

[*Becoming an Academic Writer: 50 Exercises for Paced, Productive, and Powerful Writing*](https://us.sagepub.com/en-us/nam/becoming-an-academic-writer/book244337)

### How to write a sentence by Stanley Fish

Fish's book cannot be considered a programme for writing instruction but its advice is very much one of deliberate practice.

### BASE: Academic writing capabilities framework by Helen Sword

Focuses on writing advice by analysing multiple author interviews and questionnaires. Goes againt the singular you should advice by reframing it as you may... Possibly 'you may want to try'.

Introduces the BASE framework which could be useful outside - similar to engagement frameworks - also very much deliberate practice compatible. Behavioural, Artisanal, Social and Emotional.

Artisanal was the weakest section - not because of Sword but because of the poor quality of the self reflection by the subjects (cf. King).

Behavioural and Social sections are most useful - social - writing with others, for others and among others is a particularly useful distinction.

[Air & Light & Time & Space: How Successful Academics Write by Helen Sword](https://www.notion.so/Air-Light-Time-Space-How-Successful-Academics-Write-by-Helen-Sword-ea05f21fda034f709e8f05f6c79376ce?pvs=21)
